items.body: One of the hazards of reviewing drone and ambient albums is the overuse of words like expansive. And yes, Giulio Aldinucci‘s Materia is expansive. Glad I could clear that up. It is also luminous. Another overworked adjective. But I’ll come back to that. The title translates as “Matter,” and Aldinucci has spoken of sculpting the album by removing excess material from the sound mass. Listening to Materia, that image feels entirely appropriate. Every sound appears carefully weighed, every layer stripped back until only its essential behaviour remains. Nothing feels ornamental. The opening “Not Here” is also the album’s most articulated piece. It perfectly captures the tension between accumulation and subtraction that defines the entire record. As its most dynamic composition, it could easily have occupied the centre of the album as a climax. Instead, Aldinucci places it first. It feels almost as though he says everything he wanted to say in the opening eight minutes, freeing himself to concentrate thereafter on the journey without worrying about the destination. Harmonics continually oscillate between warmth and cold while, almost imperceptibly, a melodic contour begins to emerge from what initially resembles a shifting weather system of distorted drones. There is something unexpectedly romantic about it. Full of longing, even heartache. It made me think of someone who knows they are making love to their partner for the last time. “In A Shadow of Noise” immediately begins removing material. The music becomes less concerned with harmonic expansion than with the gradual redistribution of energy inside the sound field. Low frequencies acquire greater physical presence without ever becoming oppressive, while textures slowly roughen around the edges, allowing noise to behave almost like another harmonic component. The emotional centre of the album lies in the paired compositions “Cenere e Onde Lontane” [Ashes and Distant Waves] and “Come Luce, In Sogno” [Like Light, In a Dream]. Here the appearance of distant vocalisations quietly transforms the music. If I am allowed to use the word “spiritual” in a review of a drone record, this is where Materia becomes exactly that. The voices drift in and out of focus like fragments of memory, illuminating the album from within while introducing an unmistakable human warmth. The harmonic field suddenly feels more vertical, more open, as though the music had briefly lifted itself free from gravity. “Never” redirects the album once again. It is darker, denser and less organic, concentrating on texture more than harmonic bloom. Built upon a low, persistent hum, fine granular activity continually chisels away at the surrounding texture. The closing “Sera” [Evening] feels like the natural consequence of everything that precedes it. Harmonics soften, the modular textures become increasingly delicate, and a quiet melancholy gradually settles over the music. There is no final statement, simply the impression that the material has reached a point where nothing further needs to be added—or removed. And yes, Materia is expansive. More importantly, it glows from within. To expand on the materiality of his latest album, we reached out directly to Giulio Aldinucci. In your notes you describe Materia as shaping sound by “removing excess material from the sound mass,” almost like a sculptor working with stone. How did this idea develop, and did thinking of sound as physical matter fundamentally change the way you composed compared to previous albums such as Disappearing in a Mirror or Shards of Distant Times? Ever since Borders and Ruins, and especially on the two albums you mentioned, I have always worked from particularly dense, highly tactile sound masses created through granular synthesis, from which I then structured the compositions. This approach reached an even greater level of complexity in the works collected on Materia. On one side, there is an extremely rich, dense sonic material; on the other, the need to shape it using the appropriate tools. Editing therefore became an integral part of the compositional process through the use of extremely precise static and dynamic equalizers, allowing me to work directly on the harmonic content by smoothing or removing frequencies with surgical selectivity. The radical difference between the initially raw material and the final result achieved through this process of “removal” ultimately convinced me to give the album the title Materia. One of the most remarkable aspects of Materia is its treatment of time. Although the music unfolds slowly, it never feels static. The smallest spectral shifts, changes in density, and subtle rearrangements of microscopic sonic fragments continually reshape the listener’s perception of duration. In your accompanying text you write that “time can be matter too,” capable of being shattered into milliseconds and recomposed beyond conventional rhythm. Could you talk about how this idea operates in practice? At what point does editing become composition, and how do you know when a piece has reached its final form? The parallel with sculpture, deliberately obvious, helps me explain by contrast a second concept that is actually quite distant from it. Granular synthesis allows me to treat time as if it were a material to be moulded, working at the temporal scale of microsound. A sound is split into tiny fragments (grains) lasting between roughly one and one hundred milliseconds. These grains can be layered together and played back in a different temporal order, at different speeds, volumes, and pitches. The resulting masses of grains expand and contract like countless droplets within a cloud of vapour. To put it as simply as possible: from a single voice I can create the sound of a choir. It is an extremely complex technique and also the most radical form of sound processing, because it allows control over every aspect of sound, including time itself. A sound can be shattered into fragments only a few milliseconds long and then recomposed by reorganising those fragments into a different temporal order. Returning to the sculptural metaphor, precision equalizers represent the via di levare—the process of removing material—while the grains, these temporal fragments that accumulate into layered sonic masses, embody the via di porre, building through addition. A composition reaches its final form when I can hear within it the original idea that gave birth to it. Your work has long explored memory, place, and the dialogue between environmental recordings and electronic transformation, yet Materia feels unusually tactile. Rather than evoking specific locations, the album seems concerned with the physical behaviour of sound itself—its grain, weight, porosity, and internal movement. Do you see this album as marking a shift in your artistic concerns, or is it another way of approaching the same questions that have occupied your work for many years? Both perspectives are part of Materia. Everything grew out of ideas I have been developing over many years, yet at the same time I feel I pushed those reflections to their extreme, transforming them into something different. It is no coincidence that the compositions I am working on while answering this interview are very different, as though I no longer feel the need to add anything further to the discourse of Materia. Speaking about the starting point, I feel that memory and place are both very present in Materia. There are a few quarries around my hometown, and seeing marble blocks ready to be shipped has always been very familiar to me. All the fields around my home are the exact colour of raw sienna, the pigment known in Italy as “terra di Siena” (“earth of Siena”). When the fields are ploughed or the soil is wet, the colour becomes almost identical to burnt sienna. This landscape has therefore always been part of my visual memory. With this album I wanted to let the physicality of sound speak for itself, through a play of presence and absence; geometries in which the listener may also imagine what has been removed, or what might have happened had I removed even more. Across your discography there is an extraordinary attention to detail, yet your music never feels clinically constructed. Even the most heavily processed sounds retain an organic quality, as though they possess their own internal life. You have described the interplay between organic and synthetic sound as central to your practice, but listening to Materia I often found myself wondering where that distinction actually begins to disappear. Do you still think in terms of field recordings, instruments, and electronics as separate categories, or have they become simply different states of the same sonic material? This is a central aspect of my work, both aesthetically and philosophically. Although I no longer think of field recordings, instruments, and electronics as separate categories, the analysis of each individual component has become increasingly important in my practice. In other words, these are all sound sources that must be explored with great care, never taking for granted that I already know everything about them. This is an essential step that allows me to treat them as different states of the same sonic material, a description that resonates deeply with me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Carmen Villain Memoria New Carmen Villain shares its slow-burning intensity with the Apichatpong Weerasethakul film it shares a title with Memoria by Carmen Villain Carmen Villain’s fifth album, Memoria begins in familiar territory: flute tones stretch out across an enormous, reverberant field, the same patient sound that defined her last record. It doesn't stay there long. Within a couple of minutes the ground shifts, and the record makes its real statement: this is not music built for casual listening. Sharing its title with Apichatpong Weerasethakul’s languorous 2021 film, this is a record made for the kind of slow, attentive surrender that lets its details bloom. Where 2022’s Only Love from Now On found Villain working in a spectral, dub-inflected haze, Memoria pushes that language somewhere... The post Carmen Villain – Memoria appeared first on The Quietus.

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — A different step in direction for the band after a few line up changes and a period of inactivity, the band came back with a completely different vibe, but with familiar technical speeds and playing. The attempt at moving into a more progressive sound that they tried on Scruillous is more fully felt on this album, with vocalist Rody Walker almost sounding like a different singer, with a cleaner and less punky sound to his voice. At times his range does show some weakness, but the overall passion on this album from him and the rest of the band is very potent. Lyrically being a concept album based on American exceptionalism, it is very well crafted. The track I'd recommend is From The Sky.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Last Knight is a musical project established in 1997 by Jose Medina, featuring musicians such as Marc Atkinson (Riversea, Moon Halo), Mariano Gardella, Deibys Artigas, Rafael Pacha (guitars, also with The Samurai of Prog), and Troy Donockley (Nightwish)."The Grand Overture" is a cinematic musical narrative blending classical, folk, and medieval elements?a monumental opening piece with interwoven textures. "In the Middle Ages" navigates between Alan Parsons and the Beatles, featuring a captivating melody sung theatrically by Mariano, accompanied by Sacha's poignant, arpeggiated guitar work that evokes a harsh era. "The Kingdom of Asturias" is an acoustic instrumental reflecting rugged times, with a recorder ushering the listener into a Christian kingdom on the defensive. "A War of Eight Centuries" is an anthemic, chilling interlude with Marc narrating eight centuries of conflict. "Cordoba" features Sacha's arpeggios?recalling a time when beauty and art contended with war?and vibrant Andalusian guitar. On "War," Deibys sings a tune reminiscent of Rainbow, while vintage keyboards evoke Ayreon; Nelson delivers an 80s-style guitar solo that captures the chaos. "Chivalry Tales" is an interlude driven by percussive bass and Hammond organ, with piano flourishes that skip along like knights in battle. "A Green Field of Memories" is a somber ballad, a medieval-style piece humming with acoustic notes."The Kingdom of Leon" serves as a symphonic instrumental sequel?a sweeping epic in the vein of The Samurai of Prog and Alan Parsons. It features spellbinding keyboards, Troy's bagpipes, violins, and various flutes that conjure up the world of *Lord of the Rings*, elves, and imagined medieval tales. The organ engages in a playful duel with the guitar, while the drums drive the entertaining progressive soundscape; a notable mid-song break sees the bass aggressively challenge the organ in a moment that feels simultaneously Floyd-esque, Western, and cinematic. Note the finale, where the Andalusian influence revisits the "Spaghetti Western" atmosphere to create something truly divine. "Flames Would Rise"?referencing the flames meant for heretics?features a scorching vocal performance that sends shivers down the spine. "Across the Mountains" serves as an interlude that traverses the Pyrenees on the wings of a flute melody. "The Kingdom of Galicia" offers a second epic tableau, blending folk, jazz, and world music vibes; it features a hushed, atmospheric sound reminiscent of Unitopia, balanced by Oldfield-esque Celtic moods and hurdy-gurdy and mandolin played by Sacha. There is room for furious heavy guitar work and a cinematic melting pot narrated by Mariano, acting as the resident bard. Mellotron adds a sentimental medieval touch, leading into a distinctive outro. "Pamplona" is a baroque harpsichord interlude that captures an elegiac splendor. "The Backyard" is a pastoral sketch for flute and acoustic guitar, paving the way for a cinematic finale. Finally, "Hymn for Asturias" features Deibys singing of the cycle's end?a prayerful lament that nonetheless exudes hope, underscored by Troy's flute.Last Knight?a tale of medieval glory; rest assured, this first saga will captivate you, marking the beginning of a trilogy. It is a concept of cathedral-like proportions, blending symphonic prog with exhilarating cinematic folk. A perfect example of the genre.

items.body: Review by alainPP — Side 1 opens with "Do What U Will," a surprising electro-gothic track?echoes of Ultravox with vocals reminiscent of Alice Cooper. A welcome return to contemporary rock after a six-year hiatus. "Hey Humanity" returns to a signature sound, with faint traces of Bowie and the Beatles. Colorful keyboards meet a Led Zeppelin-esque vibe?a Xavier trademark?alongside a desire to soar on symphonic elements reminiscent of ELO and sparkling guitar work. A vibrant finale featuring Queen-style guitar?magnificent, yet all too brief. "Driving To Destruction" features percussive piano � la Sheller, staccato drums, and melancholic, U2-esque guitars. It's all here: a dash of XTC and ELO, backing vocals, Supertramp-style piano, Rogue Male-style guitar, and distinctive vocal phrasing. The dynamic lyrics hint at a crash far more serious than it initially appears. "Stay With Me" follows, with vocals melting into a haughty melody amidst a blend of synth pads and keyboards. The lyrics suggest a call to action?rolling up one's sleeves to save Gaia?delivered with a Beatles-esque, crossover sound. Then comes "Charlie Knew," echoing the great Lou Reed; an epic, operatic track with symphonic orchestration. It offers a somber reflection on the times as they descend into darkness, featuring a vintage Bowie vibe and a soaring, lyrical passage that channels Cooper's madness and ELO's hope?a concentrated dose of prog.Side B opens with "Siren In The Storm," an acoustic Western-style ballad played by Kaitlin?a song of being lost amidst the waves. Captivating, narrative vocals tell the story of a siren meant to save the hero; Savannah's moving voice evokes *The Dark Side of the Moon* before a melancholic solo launches "Enigmatic Terminus." That track takes flight with sharp violins, languid vocals, and radiant, U2-style electric guitar. It is a dark, metallic tale of an approaching end, driven by a linear, martial rhythm. "Legend of Mary Jo" is a charismatic track?an old-fashioned tune with an epic, old-world duration. It tells a sad, sordid tale of love in which the heroine stays with her unfaithful husband?a parable for our own disheartened society. Originally written early in his career while playing with The Sun Machine, it is a conceptual piece?reminiscent of the Beatles and Alice Cooper?featuring classical instruments and trumpets. It has a jovial, vibrant feel?I'm sticking with the Sparks-like synth comparison?alongside a colorful, Supertramp-esque saxophone drift and a soaring, Pink Floyd-style atmosphere; a gravelly vocal cuts through a choppy, Yes-style riff and its rock-oriented variations. It boasts a distinctive sound and a solemn finale that evokes the woman's incredible destiny. A track worthy of the prog giants, featuring a blissful, final Mellotron flourish.Phideaux returns, taking his time?true to his fundamental approach. It is an epic journey best experienced in the car?a blend of psychedelic folk and progressive rock that reveals itself to be far more complex and intricate than it initially seems.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — This is a mellow, lush-sounding melodic rock instrumental album, with flashes of fusion and ambient textures around the edges. The band deliberately went for a distinctly "human" sound, avoiding excessive editing and resisting the urge to snap everything onto an electronic grid. In an age of compulsive digital perfection, there's something refreshing about leaving a little room for spontaneity?and even imperfection.Overall, this is a meditative album, ideally suited to enjoying while orbiting the Earth on a space station. There are a few moments with a jazz-fusion feel, including a track featuring electric violin, but for the most part the music inhabits its own spacious, melodic world. At times I was reminded of the solo work of Steve Howe and Steve Hackett, along with Robert Fripp, Pink Floyd, and even Pattern-Seeking Animals. But the further I got into Paradigms 2, the less useful those comparisons became. TAP seem to be defining a sound of their own.It's a little less edgy than their first album, Paradigms, but Paradigms 2 is more expansive and refined, with a broader and more varied sonic palette. It feels like a natural progression from TAP's debut, and a welcome addition to the growing body of work from this geographically separated partnership of musicians working across the USA, Canada, and England.The musicians (including several guests) are a treat throughout the album, bringing a diverse range of textures to the music. UK guitarist Suzi James (Fearful Symmetry) delivers flowing solos?sometimes with an Holdsworth-inspired flavour?along with some suitably proggy slide guitar. Texas-based Mark Cook adds the distinctive sound of the Warr guitar, mostly played fretless in the bass role. Together, they provide Paradigms 2 with plenty of instrumental colour without overwhelming its relaxed, atmospheric character.Key to the album's framework and beginnings, though, were the keyboard-based compositions Michael Jobborn sent out to the rest of the band. In a somewhat backwards fashion, the musicians took the pieces from there, massaging and developing them while gradually adding their own layers and contributions. This includes the competent and detailed drum work of Bill Bachman?whose grandfather, incidentally, was involved in the invention of the 33⅓ RPM LP.A couple of the tracks take a while to fully find themselves, including "A Hole in the Ground," although it has become one of my favourites on the album. It also features some surprisingly gentle vocals?a first for the band, although apparently not something they intend to make a regular feature.My one reservation is that Paradigms II could perhaps use a little more grit and sandpapery roughness to stretch its dynamics just a touch further. Whether that comes down to the compositions, recording, mixing, mastering, or some combination of all four, I'm not sure. I certainly can't fault the band for the achievement of putting this together largely as a home-studio project, if I have my facts straight. There's plenty here to admire. "4th Dimensional Wave" and the guitar solo work in "Wishful Solitude" provide a glimpse of what this kind of edge brings to the overall sound, adding even more texture and contrast to this spacious landscape.I can also attest that this album is a grower; the more I listened, the more it revealed itself.Overall: Paradigms II is a thoughtful, atmospheric progression from TAP's debut?an album that rewards relaxed listening and, preferably, a little distance out in Earth's orbit.4.25 out of 5 dog bones- or 4 out of 5 stars for the progarchives system.

items.album: Magdalena Ruiz

items.excerpt: San Jacinto, up in the Montes de María on Colombia’s Caribbean side, had a dancer called Magdalena Ruiz. items.body: San Jacinto, up in the Montes de María on Colombia’s Caribbean side, had a dancer called Magdalena Ruiz. The gaiteros remembered her white smile and the grace in the way she moved, and how a gathering lifted the moment she arrived: the musicians, the dancers, the drinking, the young and the old. Adolfo Pacheco remembered her too: “Si no llegaba Magdalena, se enfriaba de la gaita el son”. If she failed to arrive, the gaitas went cold. “Ahora la evoco en mi cantar”, he sings, now I call her up in my song. Those gatherings take the shape of a rueda de cumbia. The musicians stand in the middle and the women dance around them, candles in hand, long skirts sweeping the ground. Caja and gaita set the pace and the circle follows. When Magdalena arrived, that circle opened for her. “Magdalena Ruiz” opens Madre Cumbia, the album Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto, Fruko and Carmelo Torres release on 20 October through the San Diego label Bad Vibes Good Friends. Ten songs, most of them from the sabanera repertoire: three by Andrés Landero, one Torres wrote himself, the rest from writers like Rafael Pérez and Betty Ochoa. Los Gaiteros have carried the gaitas of San Jacinto since the 1940s. Fruko was the bassist and producer who ran the golden era of Discos Fuentes. Carmelo Torres took the accordion straight from Andrés Landero, his teacher and the man who made cumbia sabanera. Between them they hold most of what happened to cumbia in the last eighty years, and this is the first time the three of them have been in a studio together. They recorded in Bogotá with nine musicians in the room, Rory Morison producing and Gabriel Torregrosa directing. On “Magdalena Ruiz” the melody belongs to Iván Salcedo‘s gaita corta, the short flute a San Jacinto cumbia is built on, and Carmelo Torres answers on accordion while Fruko holds the bass underneath. Behind them, caja, conga, guacharaca and maracas keep the rueda turning, and Rafael Castro sings the lead. Listen to “Magdalena Ruiz” and pre-order Madre Cumbia HERE The post Daily Discovery: Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto x Carmelo Torres x Fruko y Sus Tesos – Magdalena Ruiz appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.artist: Talking ‘Future Sounds of Jazz’ with Michael Reinboth and Michael Rütten

items.body: Words by Justin TurfordThe iconic ‘Future Sounds of Jazz’ series has reached its sixteenth volume, an extraordinary achievement considering the Munich label Compost Records’ founder and compiler Michael Reinboth pretty much unveiled the term ‘future jazz’. This epic series of jazz-meets-electronica compilations began in 1995 and I’ve been a fan since the first edition when Michael drew the dots between artists as diverse as Luke Vibert, Patrick Pulsinger, Jimi Tenor and The Mighty Bop (alongside some lesser known names). A sonic space of jazz-infused house, breakbeats, future jazz and spaced out electronic oddities, the shared aesthetic was a jazz sensibility even if the music lived in other generic boxes. Not in a jazz sense of live improvisational musicianship but certainly in the sense of freedom, vibes, experimentation. From this early outing the world has caught up with Michael’s vision, a vision in turn inspired by Detroit’s own ‘Hi-Tech Jazz’, the Underground Resistance (Galaxy 2 Galaxy) all-time classic that revealed that jazz and electronic music could thrive together.Thirty one years after kickstarting this journey, the label returns with volume 16 and it’s another Michael (Rütten) who has been invited by his old friend to co-curate, and together they've absolutely smashed it, offering possibly my favourite volume so far with a roster that includes Momoko Gill, Trinidadian Deep, Felix Laband, Emanative & Jessica Lauren and DJ Oil.Michael Rütten is himself an essential cog in spreading the gospel about future-leaning jazz, electronic music and more. His globally-syndicated Soulsearching radio show has run for decades, he’s a music journalist, DJ and producer and has promoted key independent artists in his hometown of Frankfurt. Who better to join in the dig?I asked them a few questions on the eve of the release.. Michael Reinboth JT - Firstly, thank you for such a great compilation! Is it the best one yet? For my tastes it definitely is.Michael Reinboth - Many thanks for the compliments. Michael Rütten - Wow, that‘s a great compliment, thank you!JT - You’ve both been friends for so long and you’ve both curated many compilations but is this the first time you have compiled a record together?Michael Reinboth - Yes indeed, we’ve known each other since the beginning of Compost, and have a a genuine shared sense of taste, a journey through time.  After Vol. 15, I had a few good tracks up my sleeve but somehow not enough to fill a 3-LP / 2-CD set. That’s when Michael Rütten came along at just the right time. He had so many great suggestions that I was quite—and extremely—positively surprised, and I motivated myself to go into seclusion once again. Ha, I then found some rough FSOJ track listings on my old computer, gave them another listen, and sent my (old) ideas to Michael. Well, Michael Rütten really stepped up his game, so we currently have over 50 great tracks on our list and are already planning the next Vol. 17 for 2027.And we've decided to go on tour together and play this music in clubs, that is, to DJ. It's been a while since we've done that, and we think it's about time. Well, we're pretty good at it. After all, we have 40 years of experience.Michael Rütten - Yeah, and it happened almost by coincidence as we were talking on the phone earlier this year about potential compilations on Compost Records in the near future generally. I was relistening to some of the last ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ editions, especially Vol. 13 which Michael compiled on his own, for me one of the best ones, speaking about the selection, the flow, the feeling. All making sense. Also, I am thinking about a follow up of  ‘Soulsearching’ as it’s been quite a while. We speak on a regular basis about music, life, and what’s going on in the world of music and Compost Records. A new chapter of ‘Future Sounds Of Jazz’ has been ‘in the air’ since a couple of years, as not only there are so many new brilliant artists and tracks floating around that match with the idea of the series but also a new generation of young people discovering and appreciating this special sound of no boundaries, an open minded blend of jazz and electronics. I do feel and recognize this through my radio shows and DJ sets. So, as Michael mentioned that he could only think of two people - apart from himself - who could compile a FSOJ - one of them was me - we quite spontaneously decided to do the next edition together. Overnight we had a list of more than 50 tracks and started to sort (them) out. Which has been great fun! And apart from our dear friendship and shared love for good music I really do appreciate Michael’s attitude of ‘let’s do this’ and his open mind. And trust. As I do like his way of DJing ever since. Happy that someone just recently described us as pioneers of the DJ culture, instead of speaking of veterans ; ) We are still doing it out of pure passion. Neverending. So I am very much looking forward to travelling and sharing the decks again with Michael, spreading the music we love. Making people dance to timeless tunes of past, present, future via quite spontaneous DJ sets. No prepared set lists, always inspiring, always great fun also! JT - How did you approach the shared responsibility? Were there tracks that you had to fight over to be included or was it a relaxed process? Did you have fun?Michael Reinboth - First of all, it was a pleasure to hear each other's suggestions, it's always enriching. Then we basically gave the tracks grades, on a scale of one to three. No arguments at all. We were pretty much in complete agreement.Michael Rütten - Exciting, relaxed, open minded. Always enriching to hear each other’s new discoveries. And rediscoveries, tunes, that go a long way back and feel just right in the here and now. As we are both connected with so many artists of different genres from around the world who sent their music in and checking what’s going on daily or even 24/7 ... we both can’t just listen to everything. But tell each other about exciting new stuff. And I think it‘s a premiere that a fully analogue recorded jazz song made it onto Future Sounds Of Jazz - Brittany Davis’ ‘Sun & Moon’. Thanks to Michael’s open minded flexibility he instantly said yes to my idea. Oh, and no fights, never. FUN! JT - When you started out with the idea of ‘Future Jazz’ 31 years ago (!), there were a lot less artists operating in that way but there seems to be a galaxy full of them now. Compost and the Future Jazz compilations have undoubtedly been leaders in the development and widespread awareness of the ‘scene’ - do you recognise that yourself and have a sense of pride in your essential contribution?Michael Reinboth - The term “Future Jazz” didn’t exist in 1994 (neither as a genre nor as a catchphrase among DJs), but I wanted to give this new stylistic phenomenon a powerful (and provocative) name. Basically, it meant: this isn’t acid jazz (i.e. old stuff or old stuff played anew) but electronically produced music, mostly created by recluses in the studio, as opposed to live bands. To answer your question about whether I have a sense of pride: yes, at the very least I can claim that, with the FSOJ series, I helped found and shape this genre.JT - You have both been at the forefront of exploring and revealing the links between electronic music and jazz for decades. What has changed in your opinion? Michael Reinboth - Back then, as mentioned above, it was mostly individuals producing jazzy electronic music; today, there are far more collectives (perhaps the first being Jazzanova) that can also perform it live (the Cinematic Orchestra, for example). It always takes time (much longer for jazz than for techno) for the tracks to become more complex and sophisticated - that is, to delve deeper into the essence of jazz, discover something new, and master electronic equipment and production techniques at the same level. But there were phases when Future Jazz was flooded by Neo Disco, New Wave revivals, Trap, Lo-Fi, and Broken Techno. That was also one reason why the intervals between FSOJ events grew longer. At this point, I have to once again give a big shout-out to Michael Rütten, who really helped me get back on track with it.Michael Rütten - Many projects, bands and producers that combine both worlds (jazz and electronics) have appeared on the scene over the last 10-15 years. Probably a lot of them inspired by the likes of Jason Swinscoe‘s Cinematic Orchestra, Theo Parrish, Nicolas Jaar, Matthew Herbert, just to name a few. Contrast Trio out of Frankfurt is one of them, just re-united with a new approach, or Momoko Gill out of London, who combines classic songwriting and live played drums by herself with jazz, soul and electronic elements. Emanative aka Nick Woodmansey also produces and plays music with the live aspect in mind from scratch. DJ Oil from Marseille/Paris with his quite unique sound. So much has happened and is still happening on the forefront of music which sits somewhere in between genres. I think that the pandemic has also played a huge role regarding this point. Artists had to find a new way of expression and took the time to either re-invent themselves or/and explore new territories. Jazz is the teacher, always or let‘s say again. JT - There’s a deep and hypnotic aesthetic running throughout the compilation (with a few exceptions). This cosmic-ambient-krauty-repetition way of composition is something I’ve noticed myself a lot recently on labels like We Jazz, International Anthem and many others. Do you think that this is the natural result of a generation of jazz (and jazz-curious) musicians growing up knowing and understanding electronic music? Is it also a sign of the times? A human need to explore slowness and transcendence in an ever-crazier world?Michael Reinboth - Oh yes, I do think that slowing down and a certain catharsis - escaping this crazy world - is a reason to turn to this music more than ever. It helps; it heals a little.Michael Rütten - Well, that is something I’ve just realized while doing the tracklist for the CD/digital release of FSOJ 16! And yes, it‘s definitely a sign of the times we are living in. And also all things go round in circles. With the overload of overproduced music plus AI most recently, producers, musicians and people feel the need to slow down, dive into soul-soothing repetitive moments, going back to the roots actually. Be it via ancient rhythms, ambient (healing) sounds, it’s soulsearching in the end. Seeking warmth and something to hold on to in this mad world. Electronic music evolved out of repetitive elements, exploring of sounds and a very free approach, far from limiting forms of music theory. Bringing the human aspect more into the creation. It’s a very exciting time period right now! JT - It’s been four years since the last Future Jazz compilation which had quite a different feel to this new one - What do you see NOW that could be a new direction in another four years in the future?Michael Reinboth - It’s completely trend-independent, but Michael and I have a few older tracks with a disco vibe—disco jazz, so to speak. Let’s see if we can put together a ‘Future Sounds of Disco Jazz’ compilation with them. For Vol. 19 or 20, I could imagine something more hardcore tech-jazz.I’m curious to see how our Future Sounds of Jazz DJ gigs go. The sound has been totally underground for years and I hope that will change in four years. We’re working on it.  Michael Rütten - Like Michael Reinboth said: trend-independent is the word here. Timelessness, always forward thinking without following any trends. Just following our instinct, gut and feeling. BUY HERE! https://compostrecords.bandcamp.com/album/future-sounds-of-jazz-vol-16

items.body: This new release sets Beethoven‘s Symphonies Nos. 5, 6 and 7 beside works by Cherubini, Spontini and Rossini, to reveal parallels and influences between the two. Enrico Onofri, a conductor new to me, leads the Münchener Kammerorchester with interpretive ideas that prove both thrilling and frustrating. Beethoven & the Italians Amazon Presto Apple The program opens with an exhilarating reading of Cherubini’s Médée Overture. Although the Munich Chamber Orchestra play on modern instruments, their bowing, articulation, use of open strings, and minimal string vibrato could lead listeners to mistake them for a period-instrument ensemble. It is likely that the brass are period instruments; the timpani are played with hard mallets and the winds are well to the fore, creating a far more heterogeneous palette of color than is heard in Marriner’s middle-of-the-road performance (Academy of St Martin in the Fields/Warner Classics). Munich’s incisive and dramatic playing is more compelling. The same cannot be said of Beethoven’s Fifth. Onofri all but ignores the fermatas in the opening bars, as well as the fermata for the first violins a few bars later. Throughout the first movement, rhythmic distortions and unusual articulation are used, perhaps to create more light and shade. But this music is built on incessant, unrelenting momentum; to work against that is to ignore its basic purpose. It also negates the intended moment of calm we are meant to feel during the oboe cadenza in the recapitulation. It should be the one point where everything stops and we experience a moment of tranquility, until the rest of the orchestra rudely dismisses the idea. Here the oboe makes a full meal of it, and Onofri inserts a long pause afterward, as if the orchestra were weighing the idea of peace: again, the opposite of Beethoven’s intent. The inner movements are better, because Onofri makes far fewer interpretive interventions. He does insert unmarked swells on long notes, something Norrington and Mackerras both embraced in their first Beethoven cycles (and did not return to in their second traversals). The Trio section of the Scherzo is brilliantly played, and I like how Onofri adds length and weight to the opening three chords of the finale, giving us the chance to really hear the new sonority of the added trombones and piccolo. The first movement’s interpretive manipulations mar an otherwise exciting performance. The first movement of Beethoven’s Sixth feels fast (10’50”), though it falls within the range of several recent performances: Immerseel/Anima Eterna on Zig-Zag Territoires (10’37”), Krivine/La Chambre Philharmonique on Naïve (10’53”) and Honeck/Pittsburgh on Reference Recordings (11’01” – review). But each of these earlier readings features greater flexibility of pulse and less aggressive playing, whereas Onofri seems ruthlessly efficient. Beethoven – Symphony No. 5 – A Beginners Guide The Scene by the Brook is shaped with care, with subtle rubato and soft playing of real delicacy, but there are moments, when the violins have the melody, where one struggles to hear it in the overall texture. The Munich string section is small (the booklet lists 6/5/4/5/2 for the Pastoral), even compared to other historically informed performances: Savall uses 10/8/6/5/3 (review) and Gardiner (Symphonies 5 and 7/SDG) uses 12/10/8/6/4. Throughout the program, the strings lack the presence and power they need. The stomping energy of the Scherzo feels particularly folksy (listen out for the surprise towards the end of the movement), but the storm is curiously slow, lacking the drive and vivid pictorialism that is so often a highlight of historically informed performances. The Shepherds’ Song finale is joyous, though the braying horns and undernourished strings rob the music of any spiritual ecstasy. Beethoven’s Seventh receives the most successful performance, because Onofri offers far fewer interpretive ideas. By this point, though, the string problem felt omnipresent, a continual distraction from full engagement with the playing. And then there are “the other Italians.” Spontini’s Olimpie Overture follows the Fifth, its three-chord opening an immediate connection to the finale of the symphony. It is played with technical brilliance and arresting vitality. Onofri, to his credit, rejects treating Rossini’s Guillaume Tell Overture as “pops” music; instead, he highlights its originality and symphonic dimensions. The opening is played with real tenderness, and the trombones are impressive in the storm, but once again the strings lack presence. The final work is Cherubini’s Symphony in D major, in a performance more convincing and better played than Bellugi’s reading (Sanremo Symphony Orchestra/Naxos) or Chailly’s La Scala album (Decca). Onofri’s reading is significantly slower than both, and that extra time allows for lovely lyrical moments. The program does draw out some parallels between the compositions, but not to any revelatory degree. I would return to this recording for the performances of the Italian repertoire. Recommended Comparisons Beethoven: Symphonies Nos. 5, 6 & 7 Savall | Gardiner | Krivine | Honeck The form can be filled in the actual website url. items.body: Australian industrial electro acts Snog and Black Lung are both confirmed to make exclusive appearances in Germany in November 2026. Both acts perform at the Fourscher Festival in Erfurt on 7-8 November, alongside Mildreda, Individual Totem, This Morn’ Omina, Heimstatt Yipotash and others. Snog is centred around David Thrussell and known for left-field dancefloor tracks such as “Corporate Slave” and “Cheerful Hypocrisy,” alongside satirical, nihilistic songs like “The Human Germ” and “The Last Days Of Rome.” The group’s catalogue has been released primarily on Metropolis Records and the German labels Ant-Zen and Hymen. Onstage, Snog perform as a trio with a set described as “bizarre electro-Weimar Cabaret with an Industrial Beat.” Black Lung is a Thrussell solo act presenting the harder, darker, more experimental and techno-leaning side of his work. A new Black Lung album, “Ordo Ab Chao,” is due on Ant-Zen in late October 2026. 2026 has also seen Thrussell release “The Call Of Cthulhu”, a collaboration 2LP with Australian experimentalist Shinjuku Thief, on Metropolis Records, and the ritual ambient LP “The Reign Of Dead Matter” on Ant-Zen. About Snog and Black Lung Snog and Black Lung are both projects of Australian musician David Thrussell. Snog performs as a trio and has released a deep catalogue of industrial dance and electro-industrial material across Metropolis Records, Ant-Zen and Hymen, including reissues of remastered 1990s albums. Black Lung is Thrussell’s solo outlet for harder, more experimental and techno-adjacent material, with releases including the “Babel” collaboration with Xavier Morel and the “Armageddon” and “Euthanasia” videos. Thrussell’s 2026 output spans “The Call Of Cthulhu” with Shinjuku Thief and “The Reign Of Dead Matter” on Ant-Zen, with the new Black Lung album “Ordo Ab Chao” due in late October ahead of the Snog and Black Lung shows at Fourscher Festival in Erfurt on 7-8 November.

items.body: Lords Of Acid release “Ich Will Nur Das” (I Just Want) on Metropolis Records on 11 September 2026, the group’s fourth single of the year. The frenetic dance track features a vocal by US electronic musician Mari Kattman, sung entirely in German. Ich Will Nur Das by Lords Of Acid Lords Of Acid founder Praga Khan describes the track as “basically a love song with a serious identity crisis. The verses are pure lust: hot, dirty, aggressive and completely unapologetic. Then the chorus suddenly turns into the romantic fantasy of a lovestruck teenager dreaming about eternal love.” Kattman is a Metropolis Records labelmate and a non-German speaker who has been touring on her own recent solo album, “Year Of The Katt.” “She was perfect for this song, as it is incredibly charming to hear her American voice attack these German lyrics,” Khan said. “We didn’t want her pronunciation to be too polished or perfect, as her accent gives the track extra personality. She also understood the contradiction at the heart of the song: one minute she sounds like she wants to devour you, the next she’s dreaming about everlasting love. It’s filthy and innocent at the same time, which is pretty much Lords Of Acid in a nutshell.” “Ich Will Nur Das” follows the previously released “Karaoke Superstar” featuring Princess Superstar, “Dream Boy” featuring Carla Harvey, and “El Mundo Esta Loco” featuring Tony & The Kiki. All four songs appear on “Mundo Bizarro,” the group’s new album, which streams digitally from 15 October to coincide with part two of the “Cheeky Freaky” US tour, with LP and CD editions following on 6 November. “Mundo Bizarro” tracklist: “Dream Boy,” “Dancing On The Flames,” “El Mundo Esta Loco,” “Dopamine War,” “Maximo Roboto,” “Ich Will Nur Das,” “City Of Angels,” “So Stoned Today,” “Karaoke Superstar,” “You’re Obscene” and “A Viking’s Heart.” About Lords Of Acid Lords Of Acid formed in Antwerp, Belgium in 1988 around Praga Khan and are recognised as one of the most influential acts to emerge from the hard-edged electronic dance music scene of that era, blending techno, acid house and industrial music with lyrics on sexuality, drug use and hedonism. The group debuted with the New Beat single “I Sit On Acid,” and its debut album “Lust” appeared in 1991, followed by further releases that saw the band become a staple of the Billboard dance and alternative charts. Carla Harvey, formerly of Butcher Babies, joined as singer in 2025. Having built a global following across a multi-decade touring career, Lords Of Acid remain one of the genre’s most recognisable names, with “Ich Will Nur Das” arriving ahead of the group’s next album, “Mundo Bizarro,” streaming digitally from 15 October 2026 ahead of LP and CD editions on 6 November.

items.body: Cold Spring hosts a label night at The Globe in Glossop on 3 October 2026, with T.A.G.C., Satori, Colossloth and Llyn Y Cwn performing alongside a Cold Spring stall. Doors run from 7pm to 10:30pm, with tickets available through Resident Advisor and the event’s Facebook page. T.A.G.C. (The Anti Group Communications) was devised by Adi Newton and Steven James Turner in 1978 as a multi-dimensional research and development project. Newton uses T.A.G.C. as an outlet for his research into psycho-acoustic music, built from carefully constructed aural rituals. He is also the driving force behind Clock DVA, The Anti Group and The Future, the pre-Human League project, and a key figure in the development of electronic, industrial and experimental music since the late 1970s. T.A.G.C.’s “Iso-Erotic Calibration” is out now on Cold Spring on CD, LP and limited LP. British industrial veterans Satori formed in 1984 and have released material on cult labels including Broken Flag, Mindscan, Cold Spring and Tesco Organisation. The Glossop date doubles as the launch for Satori’s new album, “Your Life Is Worth Nothing,” which pairs harsh noise and power electronics with heavier percussive beats than the act’s earlier material. Colossloth, from the Midlands, marks 20 years as a project in 2026 and launches the new album “The Transformation And Resolution Of All Opposites” at the Glossop show. Colossloth’s music moves between brooding, abrasive passages and more transcendental material, drawing on industrial, ethnic tribalism and rave influences. Llyn Y Cwn is the solo project of Ben Powell, who has made electronic music for over 25 years, drawing on the landscapes of North Wales and his experience on Arctic research cruises. He presents “Megaliths In Dub” versus “Aniara” as an exclusive first listen at the Glossop show. About Cold Spring Cold Spring is a British independent record label focused on industrial, power electronics, noise, dark ambient and experimental music. The label has released material from artists including T.A.G.C., Satori and Colossloth, and has previously staged label nights and compilations such as the “Arise – A Cold Spring Sampler” collection. The Glossop show brings together acts from across the label’s roster, including two new album launches from Satori and Colossloth, alongside a live set from Clock DVA and Human League co-founder Adi Newton under his T.A.G.C. name.

items.body: Breton producer Quinquis (Emilie Quinquis) has announced “scenes d’interieur”, her original soundtrack to Melanie Leray’s stage production of the same name. The five-track release comes out on 13 November 2026 via Mute. The multi-media production blends theatre and film as it follows Chloe, an actress preparing to perform the role of Nora in Henrik Ibsen’s “A Doll’s House.” The stage sections trace the breakdown of Chloe’s own relationship, while a parallel story shown on film covers her childhood, raised by a mother who survived domestic violence. Ibsen’s 1879 play, which caused a scandal on release for questioning the traditional roles of men and women in marriage, runs through both timelines, tying the production to themes of control and the search for emancipation. Quinquis’ score follows the two timelines, underscoring Chloe’s vulnerability, pain and strength as she navigates the violence of her stepfather as a teenager and of her husband as an adult in the present day. She uses modular electronics to score the live theatre performances and acoustic instrumentation for the film sections, extending the dialogue between past and present that runs through the production. The single “Lena” is an intimate piece where slow-moving synths give way to distant voices as the track builds through layers of emotion. The album was recorded on Ushant Island, off the coast of Brittany, where Quinquis lives, and features a track recorded with Amsterdam-based labelmate Desire Marea, “Inkanuko.” “scenes d’interieur” (catalogue number iMUTE703) carries five tracks: “Chloe,” “Nora,” “Puzuilhan,” “Inkanuko” and “Lena.” It follows Quinquis’ 2025 album “eor” and the 2024 single “Morwreg”, both also released via Mute. About Quinquis Quinquis is the project of Breton producer Emilie Quinquis, based on Ushant Island off the coast of Brittany. Her work moves between electronic and acoustic instrumentation, built around modular synthesis, field recording and a close relationship to the Breton coast where she lives. Quinquis released the “aer” EP and the album “SEIM” before “Morwreg” preceded her 2025 album “eor,” both issued via Mute. “scenes d’interieur,” her soundtrack to Melanie Leray’s stage production of the same name, follows in November 2026 and marks her first release built specifically for a theatre production, combining her modular electronic work for the live stage sections with acoustic instrumentation for the production’s film sequences.

items.body: SPK have never made much sense as an argument for artistic consistency. If anything, their history suggests the opposite: that continuity can reside in refusing to preserve a fixed sound, method or even definition of what a musical project is supposed to be. Graeme Revell’s current work as The SPKtR extends that principle into a very different technological environment, one in which artificial intelligence, algorithmic gatekeeping and increasingly unstable distinctions between human and machine production have become part of the artistic material itself. Our conversation began with the contrasting directions currently emerging around The SPKtR and the considerably more abrasive SPKtR XXX, but quickly expanded into something larger: post-humanism, seduction as a mechanism of control, the politics of technological systems, the usefulness of unpredictability, nostalgia, artistic failure and the boundary between music and noise. We also returned to the difficult Wave-Gotik-Treffen debut and looked ahead to November’s Wroclaw Industrial Festival, where Revell intends to present something very different: not a reconstruction of early SPK, but an attempt to recover its confrontational principle using contemporary means. The SPKtR interview Karo: The SPKtR now appears to be developing along two currents: The SPKtR, where melody, atmosphere and cinematic scale seem to have more room, and SPKtR XXX, where noise and rhythm become dominant again. I find that distinction fascinating because it suggests more than two versions of the same project. Are they two different ways of acting upon the listener – one through seduction and immersion, the other through physical impact and confrontation? What can one communicate that the other cannot? Graeme: You are absolutely right. It’s still quite early in my new period of creativity and I’m not sure what the parameters and boundaries of each project are yet. As a seasoned artist who has produced music in many different styles both for SPK and for film, I feel a little bit constrained by expectations. While ultimately I will move forward and produce music that I enjoy, I am aware of the audience that has supported me for decades and I am grateful to them. So I have recreated just a few songs, whose tracks were destroyed in a fire two years ago, to show my love, but I don’t think it comes as any surprise to say that the broader SPK project was ALWAYS about change and defying expectations. Most bands play it safe at later stages in their careers by rehashing their old material to nostalgic audiences, but I prefer to live dangerously and present new material that reflects contemporary means of production and issues. So, as you observe, these are two possible new versions of the project that reflect my love for both intense rhythm and noise on the one hand and melancholic and exotic melody on the other. Because they are extremes, it is difficult to jam them together, especially in a live concert context. But there are also other manifestations as yet unrecorded, and I wouldn’t say the project has bifurcated. Karo: “The Last of Men” deals with the erosion of human exceptionalism and our increasing entanglement with technological systems. That is an enormous philosophical proposition to place inside a piece of music. How do you prevent an idea of that scale from turning the music into an illustration of a thesis? Can rhythm, distortion, frequency or the treatment of the voice carry an argument about what a human being is more effectively than words can? Graeme: Another probing question. A four-minute song is never going to be able to deliver a coherent thesis on such a subject but, as with all my music, can act as a catalyst for somewhat deeper discussion outside of the music. My use of the term Information Overload as both a warning and a prescription for dealing with the social current of the late ’70s and early ’80s is a case in point. “The Last of Men” is similarly a warning and, as you say, simultaneously aims at a constructive argument against human hubris, which is central to our survival past the very near future. Quite a lot of my music I view as a post-industrial style of “protest song”. Going even further, the involvement of AI technology takes the project into the area of “post-humanism”, which I see not as the total removal of the human from the process, a la some of Cage’s modernist work for example, but as a decentring and a redefinition of our relationship with technology. I think the song can be an effective signpost for larger issues. Karo: “La Encantadora Furiosa” introduces a rather different temperature: something darker and more romantic. It made me wonder whether seduction might actually be as important to your current thinking as technological menace. We tend to imagine our relationship with machines through fear, but the systems that transform us most profoundly are often the ones we willingly desire. Is attraction, even intimacy, becoming part of the language of The SPKtR? Graeme: “La Encantadora” is certainly a different kind of song for me but does build on my years of film scoring, where I introduced a number of indigenous musical styles into film genres. From 1985’s “Zamia Lehmanni” I discovered my love of world music and very much enjoy exploring perhaps a different take. Sometimes a piece of music is just a piece of music, but I have always agreed that seduction, especially in late capitalism, is an infinitely more efficient system of “normalisation” and submission than naked control. This is something that I have spoken about since the very beginning as a disciple of Foucault. It manifests today in the continuous dopamine hit of scrolling and has become more or less a fait accompli. Karo: There is an almost absurdly perfect SPK story in what happened to “The Last of Men”: a piece written and performed by a human musician was removed from Bandcamp after an automated system apparently identified its audio as AI-generated. Early SPK examined institutions, psychiatry, media and systems of control; today some of that authority resides in platforms, recommendation systems and largely invisible algorithms. Did that incident change the way you think about where technological power now sits, particularly when the machine is no longer simply an artistic tool but a gatekeeper? Graeme: Yes, I did it as a test of the gatekeeping actually. There are, in fact, small elements of the track that are AI-generated and I wanted to find out how good AI was at recognising itself. Quite good, as it turns out. So the incident definitely didn’t change any of my expectations. I do, however, think it is absurd that the policing of the AI content fails to take into account that the content it is flagging actually owes its existence – partially but defensibly – to the very author, myself, which it has scraped. In other words, it has forbidden the creator to re-use his own IP. Now THAT is absurd. It is a very complex ecology of power but, as with any technology, provides new possibilities while foreclosing others. The role of the artist is to expose these relationships and hopefully to go some way towards subverting them. In this case, the task is twofold: to contribute to the database more extreme content that will exist towards the outside edges of the probability distribution, and to adopt a practice of multiple iteration that allows one to favour these extremes in creating new content. Karo: I would really like to ask about Wave-Gotik-Treffen because, from the outside, that performance seemed to acquire a drama of its own. It had been conceived as The SPKtR’s live debut with Robert, and then Robert became ill and could not perform. I also understand that at one point the show came very close to being cancelled altogether. Could you take us inside what actually happened that day, and how close you were to deciding that the performance simply could not go ahead? Graeme: Yes, it was a shock and I really wanted to cancel because I knew that I could only deliver half of a show. It was only when I was begged by many people who had promoted and paid for the concert that I agreed to do my best. Perhaps it was the wrong decision, but onwards and upwards. I was lucky to have the wonderful Evi Vine accompany me on two songs, but the robot technology I had been working on could not be deployed because I was nailed to the keyboard. Karo: What interests me beyond the circumstances is what that disruption revealed about The SPKtR itself. Did having to improvise around Robert’s absence expose possibilities that a technically perfect debut might not have? Is contingency still creatively useful in a project so dependent on technology and carefully constructed relationships between sound and image? Graeme: I have always been a solo writer. Even when Neil, the original co-founder of SPK, was alive, we worked entirely separately except on stage. So my shows are tightly controlled from my workstation. Robert is in fact the wildcard improviser, so that contingency was removed by his illness and the show was the lesser for it. The unpredictability is the fun thing about live performance and the robotic element is firmly still in this territory. We will see how it goes on tour! Karo: Wroclaw Industrial Festival appears to represent almost the opposite proposition: SPKtR XXX, harder and much more rhythmically and sonically aggressive. How different should somebody who witnessed WGT expect Wroclaw to be? Are we talking primarily about different material, or about a fundamentally different relationship between sound, technology, visuals and the audience? Graeme: The two shows will be very different indeed! I think there are only about four or five songs in common and I have radically remixed them. I am looking forward to WIF because I would like to re-establish the full-frontal assault that I think I began in 1978. There are one or two contemporary acts that have taken up the mantle but overall, I have been profoundly surprised how many of my contemporaries have not come up with anything new in the last three decades. In fact, there seems to be quite a lack of exploratory energy. With respect to the WIF set, I will try to deliver a visceral experience akin to how early SPK audiences described their reaction. The ubiquity of dark imagery nowadays means it is improbable to deliver the kind of visual shock that we once did, but sonically I think the experience is light-years ahead. It is a wonderful challenge! Karo: Wroclaw also comes with a very particular audience – people steeped in decades of industrial and experimental music. Does performing in that context create an expectation around the name SPK that you feel any responsibility to fulfil, or is frustrating that expectation still part of the point? Graeme: As I said earlier, I do feel some of that responsibility, but I also look forward to confronting their inevitable reactions, some of them no doubt critical, because throwing out different ideas is always the point. I always said that this variety of approaches was the essence of what has become lumped together under the term “industrial”. The difference is that SPK invokes this variety within a single show. I hope it’s exciting and fresh rather than frustrating. Karo: You and Robert have described yourselves, broadly speaking, as composer and instrumentalist, but by now the collaboration must have moved beyond such a clean division. What interests me more is where the two generations actually disagree. Does Robert ever hear something you have constructed and tell you that it sounds too recognisably like SPK, or that an instinct which once felt radical has become historical vocabulary? And when those disagreements happen, who tends to win? Graeme: As I have already stated, I am the sole writer apart from what Rob contributes on stage. So we definitely maintain a clean division. My work process is a very long one of self-criticism, which is why releases are few and far between. As such, there can be no disagreements. He is free to offer constructive criticism and I would listen for sure. But it’s unlikely that he would, because he understands that making mistakes is all part of the joy for me. And he has his own solo project. Karo: SPK has changed so radically across its history that perhaps its real continuity was never a particular sound at all, but an unwillingness to become fixed. With The SPKtR and SPKtR XXX now taking shape, what would constitute failure for you creatively? Would it be making something that alienates people, or would the greater failure be making something audiences immediately recognise, understand and comfortably identify as “SPK”? Graeme: Absolutely, it’s about discontinuity – finding and exploring different definitions of what constitutes the boundary between what is considered music and what is noise. I would like younger generations to enjoy the music I love to create. Failure to engage beyond the wonderful fans that I already have would constitute a kind of failure. Further, though, the “post-human” project is about shifting the appreciation of art from the old ingrained tendency towards aesthetic judgement to intelligent observation of the means of production. The incredibly rapid shift in the man-machine intellectual relationship – the means of production – is the crux issue of the day and is what my art is all about at the moment. This is not an easy shift for the listener. I revel in the danger that I might alienate people because if they allow that to happen then they do not really belong in this, our space. Yet there will always be nostalgia and conservatism, and I will tell you a funny anecdote to finish. I think it was our third ever gig in Sydney in 1979. At the first gig I had hidden one hand in my sleeve and was playing the synth with a large butcher’s hook tucked into it instead. After this third gig, an earnest young punk came up to me and said, “You guys were OK, but the band hasn’t been the same since The Claw left.” About SPK / The SPKtR SPK emerged in Sydney in 1978 around Graeme Revell and Neil Hill and became one of the formative projects associated with industrial music, although reducing their history to that category obscures how radically the project repeatedly changed its own vocabulary. Noise, extreme rhythmic experimentation, electronics, performance, increasingly melodic structures and eventually the atmospheric language heard on works such as “Zamia Lehmanni: Songs Of Byzantine Flowers” all appeared under the same name. That instability is important to understanding the present project: the relevant continuity is not one particular SPK sound, but an insistence that the project should remain capable of mutation. The contemporary The SPKtR brings Graeme Revell together onstage with his son Robert Revell. Graeme remains the principal composer, while Robert introduces the improvisational element that Revell describes as the “wildcard” within performances. The music is currently developing through several possible manifestations rather than one fixed successor to SPK. Broadly, The SPKtR allows more room for melody, atmosphere and the cinematic vocabulary Graeme developed during his long career as a film composer, while SPKtR XXX foregrounds rhythm, noise and considerably greater physical aggression. Revell is careful, however, not to define these as permanent boundaries; other forms remain possible and, in his words, the project has not simply “bifurcated”. That distinction will become particularly tangible during the forthcoming European dates. The tour begins on 7 November at Wroclaw Industrial Festival, where SPKtR XXX will present the harder configuration. Revell says only four or five pieces will overlap with the material heard at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, and even those have been radically remixed. His stated intention is not to reconstruct the SPK of the late 1970s, but to recover something of its “full-frontal assault” through contemporary production possibilities. items.body: Black Lotus, the project of artist Thai, is releasing a concept EP titled “In a Room Full of Dreams” through dark synthwave, dark synth-pop, darkwave and related electronic sounds built around synesthesia, dreams, memory and perception. The title track arrives on 14 September 2026. A streaming link for the title track itself was not confirmed at the time of writing. The EP follows the earlier single “Dreams of Snakes“, already available on Spotify, and includes the tracks “When Sound Becomes Colour” and “Synthesia” alongside the title track. Geert Coppens joins Black Lotus on ‘Dreams of Snakes’ Belgian musician Geert Coppens performs as a vocal duo with Thai on “Dreams of Snakes” and has also contributed to the EP’s visual and video work. Coppens’ back-catalogue reaches into Belgium’s early minimal wave, darkwave and coldwave scenes. About Black Lotus and Geert Coppens Geert Coppens is a Belgian musician who co-founded the Micrart Group with classmate Peter Bonne in 1977, and the two went on to form the new wave band Autumn, active from 1980 to 1984. In 1982, while still working within Autumn, Coppens and Bonne began Twilight Ritual as a side project exploring a darker, more minimal sound; the pair kept Twilight Ritual a two-person project until their paths split in 1985, when Bonne went on to form A Split Second with Marc Ickx while Coppens continued designing artwork for that project and kept working under the Micrart banner. Autumn material was later compiled by Minimal Wave Records on the “Synthesize” collection, and Twilight Ritual has since been reissued on Genetic Music, Onderstroom Records and Wave Records, whose 2021 compilation “1982-2021” gathered 34 tracks spanning the project’s full history. Coppens has also worked more recently under the name Das Cabinett and, in 2023, teamed with Miami-based artist Nina Belief on the EP “In Memory Of” as Faceless 50. His appearance on “Dreams of Snakes” extends that history of collaboration into Black Lotus’s “In a Room Full of Dreams”. Black Lotus is the project of artist Thai, working across music, dance, photography, video, installation and performance-based visual art. “In a Room Full of Dreams” continues that multidisciplinary approach, pairing the EP’s concept around synesthesia and altered perception with Coppens’ contributions to both the music and the accompanying visuals.

items.body: Norwegian rock band The Largo have released their new single “Happiness“, introducing a heavier and darker chapter in the band’s sound. The track is built around riff-driven rock with roots in desert rock and the sounds of the 1960s and ’70s, while pushing the band towards a broader and more powerful sound. “Happiness” is available now on all major streaming platforms. Geir Bratland joins The Largo as a permanent member The release also comes with a line-up update. Geir Bratland, who has already been involved with The Largo for some time, has now officially joined the band as a permanent member. Bratland is best known as keyboardist with Dimmu Borgir, while electronic music audiences will also know him from his many years with Apoptygma Berzerk. With his place in The Largo now made official, he becomes part of the band’s next chapter. About The Largo The Largo are a rock band based in Oslo, Norway. The current line-up includes Jan Ole Kristensen, Alf Magne Hillestad, who also works as a drummer, producer and mixer at Velvet Recording in Spydeberg, Norway, and Jørgen Karlstrøm, joined now on a permanent basis by Geir Bratland on keyboards. Bratland played keyboards and backing vocals in Apoptygma Berzerk from 1995 to 2009, appearing on the band’s albums from “7” (1996) through “Harmonizer” (2002), “You and Me Against the World” (2006) and “Rocket Science” (2009). Since 2010 he has served as the touring and session keyboardist for the Norwegian symphonic black metal band Dimmu Borgir, contributing to the albums “Abrahadabra” (2010), “Forces of the Northern Night” (2017) and “Eonian” (2018). His permanent place in The Largo now sits alongside that ongoing work, adding a new outlet to his long-running career across Norway’s rock, electronic and metal scenes.

items.body: Salford Electronics, the project of Dave Padbury, also known for his work as The Grey Wolves, releases “Communique” on LP through Cold Spring on 9 October. The catalog number is CSR372LP, and the release is limited to 300 hand-assembled copies with a hand-stamped sleeve and a sticker seal. The nine tracks on “Communique” were written over the past decade and had previously circulated only as part of a digital-only “Communique” series that Padbury has self-released in installments since 2016. This LP marks the first time any of that material has had a physical, vinyl pressing, curated by Padbury specifically for the release. Cold Spring describes the record as “nine lo-fi electronic urban nightmares spiralling through Industrial decay, rain-drenched dark ambient, abrasive loops, brooding noise, and shards of scintillating electronics.” “Communique” runs: “Homeless” (4:06), “Tipping Point” (3:09), “Inertia” (3:27), “Collapse” (3:19) and “Restraint” (2:21) on side A; “Cellophane” (4:34), “Absolution” (4:32), “Siege” (4:37) and “Fatal” (3:48) on side B. Salford Electronics performs at the Northern Nightmare noise festival in Manchester on 10 October, the day after the LP’s release. About Salford Electronics Salford Electronics is the solo project of Dave Padbury, based in Salford, UK, formed in 2015. Padbury’s other credits include The Grey Wolves and Death Pact International, both dating back to the 1980s. As Salford Electronics, he pursues industrial ambient and techno-adjacent electronics, releasing the digital “Communique” series in installments from 2016 onward and issuing the vinyl debut “Deconstruction” through Hospital Productions in 2019, backed with remixes by Ancient Methods and Vatican Shadow. He has since recorded “Raw” (2024) and “Instability of the Signal” (2024) with Simon Fisher Turner, the latter built from Padbury’s own sound sources reworked by Turner, and has traded remixes and collaborations with Vatican Shadow, Ancient Methods, Rupert Lally and Primitive Knot, including the joint releases “Connoisseurs of Ruination” and “Primitive Knot v Salford Electronics: Remixes Volume 1.” With “Communique,” Salford Electronics moves a decade of digital-only material onto vinyl for the first time.

Macabre Masquerade by Elektrikill “Macabre Masquerade” combines new songs with reworked Elektrikill material, interludes and remixes credited to Kill Vector, Kontro
items.body: New Jersey industrial project Elektrikill, led by musician and producer Steve Vil, has released “Macabre Masquerade” through Evol Music Group. The 13-track album, Elektrikill’s second full-length of 2026, came out on September 1 and is built around a Halloween theme that runs through the whole tracklist. Macabre Masquerade by Elektrikill “Macabre Masquerade” combines new songs with reworked Elektrikill material, interludes and remixes credited to Kill Vector, Kontrol Phreak and an act billed as SPKTR. Kill Vector reworks “Ravenous” into “Ravenous (Rave Noose Mix),” Kontrol Phreak turns the “Monsters” track “(This Side Of) Parasite” into “Parasite (Darkest Fear Mix by Kontrol Phreak),” and SPKTR remixes “Drugs and Candy” as “Drugs and Candy (Trick Mixxx by SPKTR).” It has not been possible to confirm whether this SPKTR is the same act as The SPKtR, the project Graeme Revell of SPK leads with his son Robert J. Revell, or a separate, unrelated artist using a similar name. Across the album, Elektrikill moves between EBM, darkwave atmosphere, industrial-rock, electronic dance rhythms and cinematic horror, sequencing the tracks as one continuous set rather than a straight collection of horror-themed songs. “Macabre Masquerade” is out on CD and digital platforms, including Bandcamp and Spotify, with a vinyl LP edition available through elasticStage. About Elektrikill Elektrikill is the solo industrial project of Steve Vil, based in Alpha, New Jersey, and formed in 2021. Vil also works as a composer for film and television, with credits including “Grace and the Storm,” “Coma,” “The Pizza Man,” “No Clowning Around” and the theme music for the horror anthology series “Horror Shop Radio.” Elektrikill’s debut album, “Monsters”, arrived in 2023 and was named Industrial Album of the Year by NOTTHEAMP magazine. The project followed it with the EP “Propaganarchy!” (2024), the “Museum of Atrocity” EP (2026) and a contribution, “Titan of Will,” to the compilation “Electronic Saviors 7.” Elektrikill’s third album, “Küntzpiracy”, came out in May 2026 through Evol Music Group. With “Macabre Masquerade,” Elektrikill extends that catalog into a dedicated Halloween release built from new and reworked material.

items.body: There’s a whole mess of shows coming up in Vancouver, on bills featuring a fine mix of international acts and locals, some of whom we’ve seen before, and some new to our eyes. It’s a fine reminder that we’re living through a pretty healthy era for music under the umbrella of Our Thing, and while there’s no doubt a million things going on that are making touring very difficult (see Bragolin having to cancel all their US dates last week), we’re eating pretty good. Of course it’s not guaranteed to stay that way, so if you have the opportunity to go see some touring or local acts in your hometown, buy a ticket, grab some merch, try and keep the touring eco-system alive so we can all benefit from it. This pic is This pic is This pic is of Tronik (Youth) Datura Inoxia & Valanaïs, “Désir et Distance” Heavy, heavy TBM kicks and metallic programming run through the new collaborative EP from Datura Inoxia. Appearing on Ratflak, the same brutalist label which brought us the recent Blokkontroll LP, it’s a much rougher and more lo-fi version of the style the Mexican duo plies than that we associate with Berlin, but they’re drawing international producers into their grinding lockstep, including this gnarly looper done in concert with French producer Valanaïs. Datura Inoxia – Control-Represión by Datura Inoxia Wants, “Bitter Shape” Last year’s In Plain Sight was a real leap forward compositionally for Calgarian melodic new wave crooners Wants, and so we’re happy to get a sense of their next moves with a new single. Jeebs Nabil’s engrossing, winsome vocals smoothly weave through bouncy but spiky synth and guitar leads, with some raw Canadian anthemics bringing the likes of Spoons to mind. Bitter Shape by Wants Neuroticfish, “Eisbär” Neuroticfish covering Grauzone? Hell fuckin’ yeah. We’re unapologetic fans of both projects, and hearing the strong pop instincts of Neuroticfish meet the classic NDW sound of “Eisbär” is lovely. The track is taken from a compilation benefiting The White Rose Foundation, who do important educational work regarding the dangers of fascism, and our responsibility to pushing back against it. The compilation hits the streets November 6th and also features covers of welle classics from (*deep breath*) Stabbing Westward, Caustic, Leæther Strip, Nouvelle Vague, Modern English, EMF (!), The Dead Milkmen (!!), and John Fucking Carpenter (!!!). We Will Not Be Silent / Wir Schweigen Nicht – A White Rose / Weiße Rose Benefit by Neuroticfish Tronik Youth, “Touch Me, I’m Sick” Okay fine, so the italo-body music thing never quite took off the way we were hoping, it seems just as the whole thing was really starting to cook, many of the major producers veered off into NRG and other revivalist dance styles, which has a sort of historic symmetry to it at least. With that said, you still get some bangers that inhabit that not-quite new beat sound, like say this new one from London’s Tronik Youth, which has all the gnarly, mechanized funk and ominours textures you could want, while still being a righteous dancefloor heater. Touch Me I'm Sick by Tronik Youth Unconscious, “Tutto è una copia” There’s solid and unpretentious dark electro/EBM to be found on the latest single on X-IMG from the always impossible to google Italian producer Unconscious. The throwback production and slowly filtering pads feel like a nice mix of Xorcist and any number of Carpenter scores you might care to name. Also, check the B-side if you’re as much of a fan of Jesse “The Body” Ventura’s conspiracy rhetoric as we are. Cold Hearts by Unconscious Stuka, “Travelling Across Obscure Dimensions” Holy shit, what the hell is this? Best description we can come up with is baroque synthpunk about Warhammer 40k, but even that doesn’t quite encapsulate things. You’ve got the dungeon synth style medieval arrangement, and bellowed/screeched vocals paired with traditional folk singing. Even as total Games Workshop dilletantes, we have some working knowledge of the Imperium’s vast lore, but not enough to decypher this madness. Just a blast of unexpected weirdness, in the best way. Travelling Across Obscure Dimensions by STUKA The post Tracks: September 14th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.
