The final section of the album contains “Peace Prelude” and “Postludia When The War Is Over”, titles that inevitably acquire particular weight coming from two Ukrainian musicians during the full-scale invasion. Could you tell us what lies behind these two compositions, and especially the decision to imagine a musical postlude to the war while the war itself is still continuing? Has the meaning of these pieces changed for you since you wrote them? Roksana Smirnova Roksana: “Peace Prelude” was inspired by the first major winter blackout in Ukraine. I remained in constant contact with my family and was deeply worried about them, because the conditions were extremely difficult. Winter days are very short, and many people were living almost entirely in darkness, without heating or even the ability to cook. What struck me most, however, was the way people responded to the situation. They did not lose heart or give up. They remained strong and continued to believe in a better future – in the light at the end of this dark tunnel. This is the hope that “Peace Prelude” expresses: hope for light in both the literal and, above all, the metaphorical sense — the belief that light will inevitably follow darkness. “Postludia When The War Is Over” grew out of an attempt to imagine what we will feel when the war finally ends. What will we feel when the explosions and gunfire fall silent, when we look at our scorched land and realise that it is truly over? Will we celebrate and dance, will we cry, will we begin to reconsider our lives — or will we experience all of these emotions at once? This postlude is therefore not simply an image of victory or a celebratory finale. It is an attempt to hear, in advance, the silence that will follow the war and to imagine the full complexity of emotions that moment will bring. Misha: Both pieces are directly connected to the war. ‘Peace Prelude’ was written by Roksana for string orchestra during a very difficult period when Ukraine was experiencing blackouts. The piece reflects a longing for peace and, at the same time, a belief that sooner or later peace will come – a peace that can bring healing, calm and restoration. “Postludia When The War Is Over” is more contemplative. It imagines the moment after the war has ended. It is almost a narrative from the perspective of an observer who is looking back at everything that has happened – the hardship, the losses, the destruction – from a point at which the war is finally over. For me, it is a kind of silent contemplation of that experience, but at its centre there is also a deep hope and belief that, with time, wounds can heal. To imagine such a postlude while the war is still continuing is, in itself, a way of looking beyond the present moment and holding on to the possibility of an ending, of peace and of healing. The titles inevitably acquire even more weight as the war continues, but the essential meaning of these pieces for me remains connected to that hope. You are both Ukrainian musicians who have spent significant periods living and working elsewhere — including Shanghai and now Berlin. After everything that has happened since 2022, what does being Ukrainian mean to each of you today? Has living outside the country altered your relationship with Ukraine, its culture and your own sense of belonging? Roksana: I think living abroad has actually made us feel our connection to Ukrainian culture more strongly, especially when we lived in Shanghai. When you live in a very different culture, you begin to feel your own roots much more clearly. A good example is “Whispers” from our first album. The piece has a very clear Ukrainian melodic character, but we did not plan this at all – it appeared naturally and spontaneously. It was interesting to see how our own culture came through in our music while we were living so far away from it. Of course, living in other countries also brings new colours and influences into our lives and our music. But our own cultural background remains the foundation. Other influences can become part of it, but the feeling of belonging to Ukrainian culture always stays with us. Misha: Since 2022, my relationship with Ukraine and its culture has become much deeper. The war became a catalyst that pushed us to go further into our own roots and to rediscover Ukrainian culture with even greater attention – its music, its cinema and its broader artistic heritage. Living outside the country has not weakened that connection. In many ways, it has made me more conscious of it. For me, being Ukrainian today means carrying a much stronger awareness of where I come from, of the culture that formed me, and of the value of those roots. The experience of these years has expanded and deepened that sense of belonging. If you were asked to assemble a small cultural portrait of Ukraine as it feels to you right now, what would each of you choose as one book, one film, one song, one album, one play, one artwork, one dish, one building, one monument and one meme? They don’t have to be canonical choices: I’m interested in what that particular combination might reveal about the Ukraine you carry with you today. Roksana: I find it difficult to think in terms of individual books, films or works of art, because any specific choice would feel too limiting. For me, Ukraine is something I experience through its nature, sounds and smells, through the way people speak, and through the taste of its wonderful fruit and vegetables. I grew up by the sea, so my image of Ukraine includes both the sound of the sea and the steppe, as well as the smell of dry grass and sun-warmed earth in summer. I do not think any single work of art could fully capture this image. So if I were to create a cultural portrait of Ukraine, it would not be a list of ten specific things, but rather a mosaic of sounds, scents, flavours, landscapes and memories. Misha: It is genuinely difficult for me to reduce Ukraine to one choice in every category. Because we are from Odesa, so many of my strongest associations are naturally connected with the city. Rather than force a list of ten cultural references, I would choose two things that feel immediate and essential to me right now. The dish would be Ukrainian borshch. The building would be the Odesa Opera House. They are very different symbols, but together they connect something deeply everyday and familiar with the cultural memory and beauty of the city I come from.   SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 – KYIV photo by Anna Reznik Forma Formanta Could you begin by telling us about your musical background and how Forma Formanta came into being? What music shaped you growing up, when did you begin making music yourself, and how did you arrive at the darkwave and experimental language you use for this project? I’ve been involved with music since childhood. I went to music school, where I studied classical guitar. When I was around 17, I formed a band where we played something somewhere between psychedelic rock, shoegaze, and post-punk. After the band broke up, I started trying to write music on my own, around seven years ago. My introduction to experimental music began, as it often does at a young age, with an interest in the London esoteric underground. After that I just kept digging and listening to a lot of different things, but probably mostly ambient and dark ambient, drone noise, and dark folk. I’d loved things like darkwave, coldwave, post-punk, and synthwave since I was a kid — that kind of music had always been with me. But up to a certain point, I really disliked dealing with rhythmic parts. I preferred working with samples I recorded myself and with synthesizers, without being tied to a linear rhythm. I still have much more material like that, and I associate it with my om nyolc project, which doesn’t have any fixed genre direction, sound, or particular vector. If we’re talking about projects that influenced the sound which later separated into Forma Formanta, then it was discovering Hype Williams, some projects released on Northern Electronics and Posh Isolation, as well as hypnagogic pop / darkwave projects like Plecid and Tollund Men. Eventually I came to realise that what I love most is music that is extremely simple in terms of form and harmony, often with intentionally shitty recording quality. That kind of sound creates a feeling of carelessness, vagueness, and the lightness of dreams, and because the form itself is so simple, it becomes easier to work with different kinds of content within it. Zahid was recorded between Vienna and Kyiv from 2021 to 2025, spanning the period immediately before and after Russia’s full-scale invasion. You describe it as reflecting the loss of a foundation or axis — something that might be called “home” — while also connecting that feeling to a wider state of turbulence and increasing entropy. How did the album and your understanding of “home” change during those four years? Did material begun before February 2022 acquire meanings afterwards that you could never have anticipated? For a year before the war began, I lived in Vienna, where some of the first material that ended up on the album was written. It was an interesting experience, but not the most pleasant one — like almost any experience of emigration, I think. It’s natural to want to return to a sense of familiarity and stability, and generally to somewhere that feels like “your place.” With those expectations, I came back to Kyiv a couple of weeks before the full-scale invasion began. My understanding of “home” hasn’t really changed over that time. What changed is that I stopped trying to recreate it, find it, or get it back, even as a kind of fantasy. Maybe at the beginning some people still thought that things could somehow go back to the way they were, but I think by now everyone understands that there is no “before” to return to. It’s not exactly a new thought. The material written during those years started to contain more motifs of endings, finality, and completion. Not in a pessimistic sense, like everything is over and nothing good will happen anymore, but almost the opposite — as a way of living through it, making space to move further, accepting whatever happens, “learning how to swim.” Of course, this idea of “losing the ground beneath your feet,” both literally and figuratively, has accumulated more and more meaning and intensity over time. But I don’t even want to try to extrapolate what this musical material means to me personally onto the events of the past few years. Those events are too vast and too heavy, and I’m definitely not in a position to comprehend them to any meaningful extent. The liner notes compare remembering home to trying to recall a dream after waking, where details gradually disappear and imagination fills the blank spaces. That process seems embedded in the music itself: raw, muted textures in which simple elegiac melodies emerge briefly and then recede. How did you translate this movement between memory, forgetting and imagination into sound? And how do the album’s titles — from “apparition” and “death will disappear” to “sleep with armors of defeated knights” and “elegy” — fit into that world? If we’re talking about the more technical ways of moving from dream or imagination into a sonic modality, then things like distorting the original signal, using raw drone textures, or burying the vocals in noise until very little is intelligible are all fairly standard tools that have been used by many artists. Maybe the only difference is that I tried to push them into something even rawer, noisier, and more careless than is usually considered acceptable. Apart from that, I used the Soviet TOM 1501 synthesizer on almost every track. It has this very broad and deep string sound which, for me personally, is already associated with something pleasant and forgotten (and no, I don’t mean the usual nostalgia about ice cream costing five kopeeks or anything like that). As for the titles, some of them refer to words or phrases that actually appear in the tracks. They’re not really intelligible to the listener, but it matters to me what is there. The rest can come from images taken directly from dreams, or from invented, absurd combinations of words that are still meant to convey a certain image. For example, one of the tracks that carries many of these motifs of endings and completion, “moon cycle flavor mix,” got its title because I was amused by the World Ice Theory of the Austrian pseudo-scientist Hanns Hörbiger. He had this hypothesis that there had previously been four moons, three of which eventually fell to Earth, each time bringing an era to an end, destroying most living things, and beginning a new age. To this idea of global cycles, endings, and renewals, I added the name of a cigarette I used to really like and with which I have some associations, but which disappeared from sale around eight years ago: Marlboro Flavor Mix. You live in Kyiv. What is everyday life in the city like for you now, after more than four years of full-scale war? How have attacks, air-raid alerts, power disruptions and the cumulative exhaustion of the war affected your daily routines and your ability or desire to make music? At the same time, what continues to make Kyiv a place you want to live in and call home? I don’t think it would be appropriate to talk about my own exhaustion in particular. My daily routine has also remained more or less the same throughout these years. The main difference is probably that I go to concerts and other events much less often now. As for music and creativity, yes, the last two or three years have been more difficult. There’s less desire, and less enjoyment even in simply listening to the things that used to inspire me or in looking for new music. In 2022–23 I still had occasional bursts of energy — new ideas would appear, I started new musical projects together with friends, we even played some kind of post-hardcore for a while. Then, for a number of reasons, all of that gradually faded. Even though I used to love Kyiv incredibly much, it has increasingly become a place where I don’t really want to live anymore. At the moment, I simply don’t have the possibility to move elsewhere. And it’s not even mainly because of the attacks. It has more to do with the terrible transport infrastructure, roadworks that can last for years on a single stretch, ugly development (often illegal) and the destruction of green areas, parks, small public gardens, and historic architecture. The list could go on. Ideally, I think I’d probably prefer to live somewhere more rural not far from Kyiv, or in a city two or three times smaller. At the same time, I still of course consider Kyiv my home, and I hope that at some point the situation will change for the better and it will become a comfortable place to live in again. Has the experience of the past four years changed what being Ukrainian means to you personally? In terms of country, identity, and so on, almost nothing has changed for me over the past four years. I think most of my answers to those questions had already formed during the period when I lived outside Ukraine. I can’t really call myself a patriot. What I understood is simply that this is my place, and I want it to continue existing — with these people and on this territory. The main thing that exists here, and that seems to be gradually disappearing elsewhere, is freedom. Very little is regulated here to any serious extent. You can be who you want to be and do what you want to do. Of course, wartime introduces certain corrections to that, but I don’t think they are fundamental or permanent changes. I think this place quite rightfully fits the word “volnytsia” — and I’m not sure there is really an adequate English equivalent for it. It implies a kind of unruly freedom, a space where people are difficult to govern or contain. I like the fact that it is hard to call us barbarians, but we are definitely not modern Western civilization either. It is a frontier, and on many levels, not only socially or politically. There are certainly things here that are completely surreal and absurd, but at the same time it feels like one of the few places where you can still encounter something genuinely alive and real. Looking at Ukrainian music specifically, are there any albums released since 2022 that have captured the experience of the country particularly meaningfully for you — perhaps expressing something about the war or contemporary Ukrainian life that news reports and political language cannot? To be honest, I can’t point to anything specific — some complete artistic statement that really affected me in that way. Maybe this is partly because, as I mentioned earlier, I generally listen to less new music now, and things don’t affect me as strongly as they used to. In my modest opinion, there were more powerful releases and projects in the period between 2014 and 2021, also against the background of a strengthening Ukrainian identity and the political events surrounding it. Or maybe now there is simply so much happening that I can’t single things out from the general flow anymore. I’m not sure. But I’m very impressed by the overall sense of collective momentum — by the fact that under these conditions people continue doing an enormous amount of work. Experimental music in particular has developed very noticeably; before, it existed much more on the margins compared to more conventional electronic music. I like what Kyivpastrans Records and Erythroleukoplakia are doing, projects like Radio Rukh, 20ft, the regular organisation of experimental events, and the fact that there are teams bringing interesting international artists to Ukraine and organising concerts across the country, such as Obscure Bookings. I also really like the amount of attention being given to rediscovering, archiving, and popularising different kinds of Ukrainian music. Maybe this particular growth of experimental genres and events is itself an attempt to express the chaos people are living through. And perhaps that is exactly the kind of thing that neither a news feed nor political language is capable of conveying. Finally, I’d like to approach that question of Ukrainian identity from a different direction. People in Ukraine say, “This one is a Neroba,” or “This was done by Neroba” — нероба, literally a slacker, a lazy man. Nobody remembers meeting him. Some say he was responsible for early LAN fileshares in Obolon that no longer exist. Others say Neroba is a local demon inhabiting underpasses, relay cabinets and service corridors beneath the city. Our protagonist, Neroba, was part of Da Sintezatoros!, a duo from the young Kyiv electronic scene of the 90s and among the first groups to introduce experimental techno in independent Ukraine. Later, producing music for TV ads and commercial jingles, and tracks for Ukrainian pop and independent artists, Neroba slowly accumulated a catalogue of works where his name wasn’t prominent. The music on this album was created in his bedroom studio between 2010 and 2020. A blend of boogie, funk, house and disco – 12-bit drums programmed on his beloved Casio RZ-1, alongside the usual suspects: a Roland JV-1080 and a Yamaha DX7, a couple of drum machines and a cheap early-90s Boss SE-50 stereo effects unit. Neroba’s small synth sanctuary translated the mood of the city at a specific hour. The artist currently lives in Kyiv. We are happy to present his debut solo work. This album is by Neroba.   Motorpig ~ We Inherited the Ruins We Inherited the Ruins Things are made slowly. Wood is polished. Surfaces are worn down. Instructions become meaningless. The archive burns. Somewhere beneath it all, the machinery continues to hum. A study in repetition, friction, manual labor, and whatever remains after progress has left the room.   Oleksii Podat ~ We Were Born To Feel Everything A long-form composition knitting sundry paraphernalia of intimate value into a tēla that feels as recognisable as it is unhinged — akin to the stroke of a reliable brush tilting just enough to unveil the mesh of the fabric, only to skid into another aberrant tangle.   Doctor Bugg ~ REM REM – Rapid Eye Movement – is the phase of sleep during which a person dreams. In this state, reality feels fluid, surreal, and dissociated. Doctor Bugg explores REM through fragmented memories, a sense of lost time, and liminality. REM focuses on the instrumental canvas. The composition features percussive electronic sounds and jagged, disorienting textures that intertwine with guitar and processed saxophone recordings. With this release, the artist changes course, moving away from a focus on lyrics. Genre spectrum: industrial electronics, experimental hip hop, spoken word, and improvisation. “Listening is a very personal experience. It’s best to listen to this music without worrying about how it might be perceived by someone else” – prescribes Doctor Bugg.   Alex Malch ~ In a Landscape 5 years ago, in 2021, Alex started writing this album and after multiple unsuccessful attempts to record it I have finally finished the project This album has everything he wanted and needed to say, musically and lyrically, and he don’t intend to release any more solo music.   Vøvk, КАТ ~ Split (Live @ Druk, Kharkiv, 17.05.2026) This live split captures our joint performance by Vøvk and KAT, recorded live on May 17, 2026, at a show in Kharkiv organized by the KAZKA Family community. The release features four tracks: Vøvk presents ‘Sil’ and ‘Leleka’ from last year’s album ‘Litera’, while KAT contributes ‘Lyst’ and ‘Bez Pravyl’ – the latter recorded in Ukrainian for the very first time. For KAT, the evening was particularly meaningful, marking their first live performance in their hometown of Kharkiv in three years. “For years, we wanted to organize a show together with KAT, but for various reasons, it just never happened. When this spontaneous gig in Kharkiv came up, we decided to make the absolute most of it. The idea for the release came together quickly: we felt we had to capture this special day and time together. Especially in one of our absolute favorite cities.” — Vøvk We are releasing this split as a Bandcamp exclusive, available solely for streaming and purchase on the platform. All proceeds from sales will go directly to the ongoing fundraiser by the KAZKA Family community, supporting those who make events like this possible in the first place. “We always love playing alongside our friends in Vøvk, and this show happened completely spontaneously. Even though it was our first time performing in three years, we jumped at the opportunity to capture May ’26 in Kharkiv with this short live split. We want more than just dark memories to remain from these times; we want Kharkiv to stay alive and thriving. Intimate initiatives like this – which was Vøvk’s idea – are simply priceless.” — KAT   Serhii Litinskyi ~ Fernstimmen The musical practice common in the time of Ockeghem and Josquin has disappeared from our present-day musical protocols, in which the listener’s customary connection to music is organized linearly. This is symmetrical to the way in which music, in turn, connects to the listener. Today, it is difficult even to perceive the difference between these two connections, but once there was an enormous distance between them. A singer taking part in the performance of a Josquin Mass presupposed a trajectory of sound that did not lead to the listener, because the figure of the listener did not exist in the church in the first place. Even when members of the congregation were present at the service, the singers were either isolated from them or turned away from them; combined with the church’s powerful reverberant acoustics, this effectively deprived the congregation of the possibility of perceiving the music. If we set aside the liturgical function and the metaphysical dimension of the process, and consider instead the physical and physiological dimension of musical practice, music here returned to itself, existing in a reflexive loop. The sound produced by the singer returned to the singer and shaped a state in which he could produce sound that was even more effective at producing the state in which effective sound could be produced. The circular trajectory of the music enclosed and isolated the musical material. When we encounter Josquin’s music, we immediately register the autonomy and coherence of its sonic construction. In terms of expression, it is alien to the kind of expressivity we habitually describe as a reliance on an outward effect. When we listen to Josquin’s music today, we connect to it asymmetrically. The singers’ voices always seem to come, so to speak, from afar; they do not address us directly. We always listen from the side, in a sense eavesdropping, witnessing the circular trajectory of the music and the effect that sound, through the singer’s body, has upon itself. In working on this piece, I sought to reproduce this ancient circular trajectory of sound. This also determined the insufficiency, and ultimately the inadequacy, of a linear algorithm in which the score is realized in a single act: a direct performance, fixed in a recording and aimed at the listener. I needed to submit to the effect of the sound and, in turn, affect it under the influence of that effect. Having accepted these rules, in the course of realizing the piece in sound I substantially altered and supplemented the performance of the original score with sounds of different origins. In other words, I intervened in its realization by virtually every means through which a composer can directly influence the sonic result—from field recordings to sound samples, to the creation of autonomous musical structures and events within this new sonic environment. These almost always conceal the initial material, making it nearly indistinguishable within the texture of the final sound. Nevertheless, it was precisely this initial impulse, at the origin of the circular trajectory, that determined the character and rhythm in which the spiral of this music unfolds. I am sincerely grateful to all the musicians through whom Fernstimmen—“distant voices”—have come closer.   DJ POPS ~ между частотами The label ERYTHROLEUKOPLAKIA out of Kyiv presents itself in a raw, punky style, but this second album from associate DJ Pops is altogether more considered and delicate than you might be expecting. It’s another one with IDM/braindance irregularity at its core, but it’s definitely got more emphasis on the “dance” side of the equation; so no matter how lopsided the grooves might get, they nonetheless are grooves, and hold the attention and the body locked in. It also, however abstract it gets, feels weirdly un-digital—like constructions of wood, string, rusty metal, tape, and glue, sometimes with little creatures running around inside them. [Bandcamp Daily]   MIXES   VIEWING ROOM (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are classic bands whose lineups become fixed in time, beyond any later variations, as the very ones through which we first discovered them; these are the lineups that produced a handful of classic albums, creating the impression (or illusion) that they could do no wrong. This happened with the Peter Gabriel-era Genesis in the 70s, with Yes during the time Bruford and Wakeman were in the band, and in many other cases, given that the decade was so rich and vast it seemed endless, and it happened with Roxy Music. However, what set Roxy Music apart was that, alongside Bryan Ferry, possessing a voice that was glamorous yet capable of sounding menacing when needed, and Andy Mackay (on sax and oboe, coaxing out an incredible sonic range), and Phil Manzanera (a guitarist who possessed undeniable credentials in an era when every self-respecting guitarist had to prove their worth), and Paul Thompson (on drums, anchoring a sextet with such great chemistry), there was Brian Eno. He was the element that would disrupt any sense of equilibrium, or, conversely, help them find balance within the very imbalance that made them unique."Re-Make / Re-Model" kicks off without asking for permission; Manzanera's guitar seems to attack, and the same goes for Ferry's vocals, almost punk before punk existed. They sounded frenetic, with McKay's sax channeling free jazz, and were expertly backed by Graham Simpson's bass. Brian Eno's signature backing vocals and synthesizer interventions were already present; he brought the electronics, he brought modernity. You can sense the freedom and the way they play around with interruptions (including a nod to the Beatles) during the pauses before the finale. Ferry was not just a singer with a distinct personality; he also contributed significantly on the piano with his dissonant notes. They had fun experimenting in the studio, and that spirit was captured on the record; the proof is that it sounds like a live album."Ladytron" opens with a space-rock feel; Mackay's oboe displays a subtlety echoed by Ferry, revealing a facet of the band completely different from the previous track. The sound then seems to shift toward the Canterbury scene, with the saxophone and guitar sharing the lead, at times epic, at others drifting aimlessly without vying for the spotlight. "If There Is Something" surprises with a country-western atmosphere, yet the band transforms it into glam rock in the vein of Bowie or Elton John; then, Manzanera's Black Sabbath-esque solo tears us away from the Wild West, while Ferry sings as only he could, at times reminiscent of Family's Roger Chapman."Virginia Plain" would become one of the band's classics from this early period, featuring the humor in Ferry's vocals combined with Eno's synthesizer work, all within a track that remained, at its core, rock 'n' roll in their own distinctive style: an avant-garde approach devoid of solemnity, which is precisely why we still love it so much.The wonderful thing about this debut was its variety; as we shifted to something more serious and experimental with "2HB," Ferry's voice transported us to space epics and evoked a yearning for a bohemian past, something he harbored even in his youth at the time, which also gave the band a modern edge. Paul Thompson varied the rhythms, introducing more syncopation, while the saxophone's intensity receded, leaving Eno's keyboards to persist, looping over and over, and making us feel as though we were inside Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.We are talking about space, and it feels as though we are plunging into a black hole of unknown destination; "The Bob (Medley)" kicks off, following the intro, with an epic rock sound driven by saxophones reminiscent of Van der Graaf Generator and Ferry's defiant vocals. Then comes a medieval section, echoes of the past, fitting for a band as cinematic as Roxy Music (especially during this era) followed by raw, wild rock, yet punctuated by synthesizers that feel like blocks of ice in the desert, alongside Mackay's frenetic oboe. And when Ferry's piano notes arrive, and the guitar soars like thunder in a storm, making its presence powerfully felt, we know this band is like no other."Chance Meeting" is one of those very special tracks that seem not to have been composed on Earth, possessing a strange beauty and a strange melody; it certainly resembles contemporary classical music, dissonant and asymmetrical, with an architecture that defies established conventions. This is because the piano and Ferry's calm, simmering vocals contrast with Manzanera's guitar, which cuts through the air like a power saw.If you think Would You Believe settles into calm and normalcy, you are mistaken; Ferry's obsession with nostalgia takes us, for the first time, though not the last, back to the 50s, but in a wild, street-level style."Sea Breezes" once again pushes the boundaries of the avant-garde with an Eastern-tinged melody where Ferry's voice takes center stage, shining like the marquee lights of an old theater in a seaside town where seagulls bear eternal witness to the people passing through year after year. The music conjures images and stirs emotions; it seems to repeat itself yet introduces subtle shifts, unfolding slowly, like the passing years, almost imperceptibly. Beneath the layers of wildness and impetuosity lay wisdom and deliberate structure; Paul Thompson knew exactly when to make his entrance, and just as the oboe plays a delicate melody, Manzanera cuts through it with his guitar, creating a harmony born of chaos. When Ferry sings, it is as if he is backed by a strange orchestra, strange, indeed, but an orchestra nonetheless.Precisely by downplaying an era that seemed to be growing increasingly serious, they conclude with a simple, almost a cappella melody titled "Bitter's End", a tune reminiscent of an old village, quintessentially English, fully aware that every avant-garde movement follows its own unique path.

items.body: Review by Alxrm — The beginning of the real Rush - no offense to John Rutsey and the debut album which I really like- but Geddy and Alex ever since were aspiring for a deeper sound and a more progressive direction which didn't appeal to John. This is made plain even from the intro of the opener of the album which actually was the jamming they did together when Neil was auditioning for the band. Even though the music remains essentially rock and most song durations are around the three-minute mark, the first twists and turns make the presence felt. More than that, acoustic (Fly by Night, In the End) and classical (Rivendell) guitars are tastefully used to widen their palette of sound. However, the key-track on the album is the suite By-Tor & The Snow Dog because its complex structure would become their compass for the future where they would go off their pure rock roots entirely.Compared to the debut, the listener can easily perceive the growth the band underwent within such a short amount of time. The unstrained enthousiasm is replaced by deeper and at times more complex compositions showing clearly that the boys would not content themselves by repetition. Moreover, the new guy would become their standard lyricist and would go down in history as one of the best of all time. We should thank our luck that their paths were crossed.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — If you have followed my reviews spanning the prog folk diaspora, you'll know there is nothing I welcome less than another version of "Scarborough Fair", with which particularly Nordic groups seem disproportionately enamored. It therefore follows that I cannot recommend an album in which arguably the best track is in this single-song sub genre. Sadly this is the case for the extinct-on-arrival dinosaur known now as the "Kaarmesormus". It might garner 3 stars from a new group just based on the continued mellotron blasts but not from esteemed veterans like KOSMOS, and, while each number could be a supporting cast on a better album, this isn't that. From the soporific first half to the plodding and equally exhausted faux metal second half with its SSRI-free spoken interludes, this is all a big downer, and I do normally appreciate the authentically morose. If I had to pick a couple they would be the opener and "Kielletyn hedelm�n tarha", but both are essentially submerged in their surroundings. Like a therapist once said to a friend who cried incessantly through the first few sessions, "you need a good drug". Start anywhere else and let this one slither off to the side until you are emotionally ready. 2.5 stars rounded down.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Undoubtedly one of the great surprises of this year is the release of King Gizzard's full-blown EDModyssey 'Alien Metal', which is their twenty-eight studio album to date. The follow-up to 2025's'Phantom Island' sees the Australian band abandoning all rock instrumentation for a futuristic beat-driven, techno-inspired rave sound, utilizing a modular synth system that allows them to explore avast range of sequenced rhythms, electronic textures, and an overall synthetic, club-orientedproduction style. Contemporary bands rarely do such dramatic stylistic shifts, but this acid-ladencreation from the kings of psychedelic blues turns out to be a fun and engaging listen (that willnevertheless shock many dedicated fans), that is above all else, a finely constructed electronicwork, wherein each tracks flows into the next one, giving the impression of a massive piece ofprogressive house. Within this mixture of quirky techno beats, bassy breakbeats, and ambientinterludes, the ominous alien-like robotic vocals that wiggle their way through, give 'Alien Metal'somewhat of a sci-fi edge. However, despite all of the pristine synth sequences and polished studiosound, the occasional repetitiveness of this album can potentially lead to listener fatigue.Moreover, the synthetic club feel provides for a great background listen, but is there really thatmuch substance to dig into upon repeated listens? The tracks that I enjoy the most on 'Alien Metal'are the punchy opener 'Sapience', which beautifully transitions into the excellent title track,followed by the powerful and mesmerizing 'Level 5', and the trippy 'Uqt', which appears towards theend. The album finale is strong, too, while the entire work feels intentionally futuristic andvibrant, which is perhaps what most listeners would cling to.

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — This might be the first time I have not been taken aback by a new Mastodon album, simply because theexpectations have been exceedingly high this time around. A reflection upon the dramatic passing offounding member Brent Hinds, following his departure from the band earlier, 'Marrow Deep' is arecord exploring grief through a variety of dense and ominous sounds. This is not necessarily areturn to the extreme and primal energy that had shaped the Atlanta-based band's early records, butit comes close to being their most straightforward metal album in years. Having added touringguitarist Nick Johnston and keyboardist Jo�o Nogueira to the lineup, this five-piece version ofMastodon is intriguing, but it lacks the untamed songwriting of Brent Hinds and his overtlypsychedelic undercurrents. For this reason, 'Marrow Deep' is somewhat less adventurous thanpreceding releases from the band, even if it preserves the sludge-informed prog metal framework thatlisteners have become accustomed to. It just feels solid all throughout but without significantpeaks.Production-wise, this album is strong but not groundbreaking, with the heavy guitars occupying mostof the mix. I do, however, vastly enjoy the prominent contributions of the band's full-time keyboardplayer, whose playing provides a beautiful atmospheric backdrop to the otherwise ravaging guitars ofBill Kelliher and Nick Johnston. Interestingly enough, there is a greater highlight on melodictextures and sombre passages on 'Marrow Deep', that had only been superficially explored on 'Hushedand Grim'. Nevertheless, this new Mastodon record feels meandering without really having any weakmoments. Highlight tracks like the fast-paced 'Snakes for Dinner', the ritualistic sludgy number'They're Coming for You', and the tasteful but melancholic song 'The Vanishing', featuring GeezerButler and reminiscent of the great 'Planet Caravan', are perhaps the only moments worth lookingforward to upon repeated listens, while monotonous heavy numbers like 'Poisonous Weapons' and 'Inthe Ruins' lack the novel and mind-bending edge that used to make each new Mastodon something toanticipate.Longtime fans of the band will discover heaps of excellent, wild and turbulent riffs here, while theenjoyers of the band's progressive leanings shall be pleased with the haunting keyboards appearingon 'Marrow Deep'. Consistent and straightforward, this record hardly reinvents the Mastodon sound,which is very likely why it doesn't fully click with me.

items.body: “Tadzungaira” is one of the old Shona mbira pieces, played at ceremonies when a family calls on its ancestors to end a run of hardship: a drought, a stretch of poverty, a season where nothing comes right. The word means we are lost, and some traditional players refer to the piece as “Todzungaira”, others as “Muroro” or “Nehondo”. The Mbira Renaissance Band played it at Paper Birch Books in Edmonton on 21 February. They have reached for the word before: “Daira”, from their 2018 album Famba, has the line “Tadzungaira, tadzungaira musango”, we are tired, we have been wandering in the forest a long time. The song opened their session for the Pocket-Sized Series, a monthly recording run by the band’s drummer, Tony Flanagan, made among the shelves of the bookshop and released as video, modelled on Tiny Desk and funded by the Edmonton Arts Council. The Mbira Renaissance Band came out of the Canadian city’s music scene in 2013, started by mbira player Chaka Zinyemba with bassist James Stuart. Chaka and lead singer Chiedza Zinyemba are from Zimbabwe and sing in Shona, with Chiedza also on hosho and congas. George Koufogiannakis plays guitar and brings thirty years of jazz behind it, Flanagan drums, and Munya Viyali is on keys. Their repertoire sets the mbira alongside jazz, reggae and afro-pop, and the songs are usually about family and coming together. They toured Zimbabwe for the first time in July 2025 and released the album Roto the following January: half of its eight tracks carry a horn section with parts written by Koufogiannakis, “Zunza” brings in West African djembe from Reckie Lloyd and closes on mbira, and “Mufaro” features the Afro-Cuban duo OKAN with pianist Jeremy Ledbetter. Stream, listen to and get your copy of Roto HERE The post Daily Discovery: The Mbira Renaissance Band – Tadzungaira appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: The piano has always occupied a peculiar position in contemporary music. It can function as a harmonic instrument, a melodic voice, a percussive object, or simply as a source of resonance and noise. In recent years, the felt piano has increasingly become associated with the latter possibilities: its softened attack and reduced brightness reveal a more intimate and fragile side of the instrument. Intimate Felt Piano, by Mondo Loops, takes this idea as its starting point, but rather than presenting the felt piano as a single predefined aesthetic, it treats it as a collection of textures that can be shaped by the player. The instrument is based on a double-felted Kawai KU3B upright piano, sampled across 88 keys with three velocity layers, pedal-up and pedal-down sampling, and up to four round robins. It is designed around a close, warm sound rather than the polished projection of a concert grand.  That choice immediately defines its character. An intimate piano The first impression suggested by Intimate Felt Piano is one of physical proximity. The instrument does not attempt to recreate the experience of hearing a piano from the back of a concert hall. Instead, it places the listener much closer to the mechanism. This is particularly evident in the way Mondo Loops treats the noises surrounding the notes. Felt noise, pedal release, hammer release, and room/player noise are all independently controllable. These elements could easily have been treated as unwanted artefacts of the recording process. Here, they are deliberately exposed as part of the instrument’s sonic vocabulary.  It is an important distinction. The noises of a piano are normally something that a sample library tries to reproduce convincingly while keeping them subordinate to the musical note. Intimate Felt Piano instead allows the user to decide how prominent those sounds should become. As a result, the instrument can move beyond the traditional idea of a piano library and towards something closer to a playable sound-design tool. Three ways of hearing the same instrument The library is organised around three sample sets: Felt, Tape and Mute. The Felt layer represents the most direct interpretation of the instrument: a double-felted upright with a soft and restrained response. Tape takes the concept somewhere else. The material is recorded to tape, slowed slightly and retuned, creating a denser and more nostalgic character. Rather than simply adding tape processing to an otherwise conventional piano, this approach makes the altered recording itself part of the instrument’s identity.  Mute is perhaps the most conceptually different of the three. The strings are physically muted, producing a tighter and more percussive response. Together, these three approaches make the instrument considerably more flexible than its name might initially suggest. They can be understood almost as three different perspectives on the same object: the piano as an acoustic instrument, the piano as a degraded recording, and the piano as a percussive mechanism. The sound between the notes The most interesting aspect of Intimate Felt Piano may not actually be the piano itself. It is what happens between the notes. The interface provides controls for Felt, Hammers, Pedal, Noise and Round Robin behaviour, alongside independent controls for the Room, Ribbon, stereo Pair and Pad elements. The microphone setup includes stereo condenser, ribbon and room perspectives.  This gives the user considerable control over the perceived distance and physicality of the instrument. A close microphone can make a sparse melody feel almost tactile. Increasing the room component can turn the same material into something more atmospheric. Mechanical noises can remain almost imperceptible or become an audible layer in their own right. For composers working with sparse material, this is particularly useful. When a piece relies on repetition, sustained tones, or limited harmonic movement, small changes in resonance and articulation can become structurally meaningful. The sound of a pedal being released or a hammer returning to position can provide information that would otherwise be absent from a perfectly clean MIDI performance. The imperfections are therefore not merely imperfections. They become parameters of the composition. From neoclassical to sound design Mondo Loops positions the instrument towards lo-fi, ambient, cinematic, and neoclassical music, and these are certainly natural environments for it. However, its possibilities extend beyond those genres. A felt piano is particularly effective when the distinction between instrument and texture becomes blurred. A simple repeated figure can be left almost completely dry and intimate, allowing the physical sound of the piano to remain exposed. Alternatively, the Tape or Mute material can become the starting point for further processing: granular synthesis, convolution, filtering, delay, or extensive reverb can transform the piano into something increasingly distant from its acoustic source. This makes Intimate Felt Piano potentially interesting within experimental and electroacoustic workflows as well. Rather than requiring the piano to remain recognisable as a piano, the instrument provides enough raw material to allow that identity to be gradually dismantled. Imperfection and repetition There is also something particularly appropriate about this approach in the context of contemporary minimalist and post-minimalist writing.Repetition inevitably draws attention to details. When the same harmonic or melodic material returns multiple times, the listener begins to notice differences in attack, resonance, noise and spatial perception. A perfectly identical repetition can sound mechanical; a repetition containing small variations can instead suggest the physical passage of time. The combination of multiple velocity layers and up to four round robins helps avoid a completely static repeated performance, while the dedicated noise controls allow the user to decide how much of the physical character of the instrument remains audible.  In this sense, Intimate Felt Piano is not only concerned with making a piano sound softer. It is concerned with making the process of playing the piano audible. A deliberately focused instrument There is a temptation with modern virtual instruments to judge them according to how many sounds they can cover. Intimate Felt Piano takes the opposite approach.It is deliberately specific. This is not a comprehensive piano collection intended to reproduce every possible performance style. Its identity depends on the particular combination of felt, mechanical noise, close recording, and restrained dynamics. That limitation is precisely what gives it character. Instead of attempting to replace a general-purpose piano library, it occupies a much more specific space: the piano as an intimate, imperfect, and malleable sonic object. At $35, Mondo Loops also positions it as an accessible addition for producers and composers who already own a conventional piano library but are looking for a more defined sonic personality. The instrument runs in the free Kontakt Player 8+, so no additional Kontakt purchase is required.  Final Thoughts Intimate Felt Piano is most convincing when considered not simply as another felt piano, but as an exploration of what happens when the secondary sounds of an acoustic instrument become part of the musical material. The soft attack is only the beginning. Felt, hammers, pedals, room ambience, microphone perspective and tape degradation all contribute to an instrument that can occupy several different positions between piano and texture. For contemporary composers, producers and sound designers, this is perhaps its most valuable quality. The piano does not have to remain a transparent vehicle for harmony or melody. It can become an object to be examined, repeated, degraded and reshaped. And sometimes, when the musical material is deliberately minimal, the sound surrounding the note becomes just as important as the note itself. mondo loops product page here’s a demo mede entirely Intimate Felt Piano: Davide Fasiello · Davide Fasiello – broken memoriesThe post Mondo Loops – Intimate Felt Piano: When the Piano Becomes Texture first appeared on Modern Classical Music.

items.body: Dusken Harmony, the dark synthpop and twilight electronics project of Minsk-based multi-instrumentalist Anton Yeroma, releases its new album “Unkeyed” on September 16, 2026, as a nine-track digital release on Bandcamp. Unkeyed by Dusken Harmony ‘Unkeyed’ tracklist and concept “Unkeyed” runs across nine tracks: “The Golden Weight”, “In the Walls”, “Another Face”, “The Sculptor’s Flaw”, “Open the Box”, “The Little Prince of the Night”, “The Secret Flower”, “Lighthouse” and “The Locked Room”. Dusken Harmony describes the album as sitting at the crossroads of dark synthpop and twilight electronics, built on haunting vintage textures, and as a story of artificial isolation, toxic attachments and the search for a flicker of inner light in a world of polished facades. The album is available as a digital release on Bandcamp, with a full links hub at band.link/unkeyed. About Dusken Harmony Dusken Harmony is a musical project run by Anton Yeroma, a multi-instrumentalist based in Minsk, Belarus, blending new wave, post-punk, darkwave and dark synthpop elements. The project’s Bandcamp catalog began with the EP “Disarmed”, released August 14, 2024, a six-track collection paired with the music video for “The Shadow”. “Thorny Agony” followed on May 20, 2025, a nine-track album that included a video for “Black Mask”. “Unkeyed” is the fifth release in Dusken Harmony’s Bandcamp catalog, following “Disarmed” and “Thorny Agony” as well as two further releases, “Shrouded in Mystery” and “The Last Star”. The new album extends the project’s dark synthpop and twilight electronics sound into a concept built around isolation and the search for light within it.

items.body: Italian gothic rock, post-punk and darkwave quartet Christine Plays Viola kick off a Spain and UK tour on 11 September 2026, opening in Barcelona before three nights in Spain and four shows across the United Kingdom through 20 September. The run follows the band’s 2026 album “F.I.V.E. (Fear Increases Violent Emotions)” and its singles. Ticket arrangements are handled by the individual venues; the 18 September Shropshire show is confirmed as free entry. The Spanish leg runs Barcelona, Madrid and Valencia with local support acts each night. In the UK, Christine Plays Viola play London, Shropshire, Morecambe and Gateshead, including a slot at the Bats in the Attic Festival in Morecambe. Tour dates for Christine Plays Viola 11 September – Barcelona, Spain – Sala Freedonia, with Darklands 12 September – Madrid, Spain – Cadavra, with Last Dusk 13 September – Valencia, Spain – Black Note Club, with After Mankind 17 September – London, UK – The Hope & Anchor, with Long Night and Last Dusk 18 September – Shropshire, UK – Percy’s Café Bar, with DJ SyncroMystic (free entry) 19 September – Morecambe, UK – Alhambra Live, Bats in the Attic Festival 20 September – Gateshead, UK – The Black Bull, with The Exceptional Mr Hyde About Christine Plays Viola Christine Plays Viola formed in 2008 in Abruzzo, Italy, around an idea by guitarist Fabrizio Giampietro and drummer Daniele Palombizio, joined shortly after by bassist Desio Presutti and a singer known as Christian. The band released its debut album, “Innocent Awareness”, in 2011, followed in 2014 by “Vacua”, a record inspired by Spanish painter Francisco de Goya that anchored the group in the darkwave and new wave scene. The current lineup features Giampietro on guitars, synth and programming, Massimo Ciampani on vocals, Gianluca Orsini on drums and Marco Di Ianni on bass. The band’s fifth studio album, “F.I.V.E. (Fear Increases Violent Emotions)”, was released on 19 January 2026 through Cleopatra Records. Christine Plays Viola supported the album with the single “Desolate Moments” in April 2026 and the standalone track “At Last, I Found You” in July 2026. The Spain and UK dates mark the band’s first live run since those releases.

items.body: Australian industrial synth crust artist Schkeuditzer Kreuz, the solo project of Kieren Hills, returns to Japan and Southeast Asia in October 2026 for a 21-date run across seven countries in 24 days: Japan, Cambodia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines. Ticket details are handled by the individual venues and promoters; several Southeast Asian stops are listed with the venue still to be announced. The tour opens in Tokyo on 2 October and works through Nagoya, Shizuoka and Osaka before crossing into Cambodia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines, closing in Dasmariñas, Cavite, on 22 October, with three further Indonesian dates following on 23 to 25 October. Stops include the Visayas Hardcore Punk Fest in Bacolod City and a Bali date at Gimme Shelter. Tour dates for Schkeuditzer Kreuz 2 October – Tokyo, Japan – Earthdom 3 October – Tokyo, Japan – Ochiai 4 October – Nagoya, Japan – Duct 6 October – Shizuoka, Japan – Sougen 7 October – Osaka, Japan – Hokage 8 October – Siem Reap, Cambodia – Atlantis Metal Bar 9 October – Phnom Penh, Cambodia – Distortion 10 October – Chiang Mai, Thailand – Yoda Gallery 13 October – Bangkok, Thailand – Live Haus BKK 14 October – Singapore – venue to be announced 15 October – Batam, Indonesia – Loka Suara 16 October – Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Moutou 17 October – Bacolod City, Philippines – Visayas Hardcore Punk Fest 18 October – General Santos City, Philippines – venue to be announced 19 October – Davao City, Philippines – venue to be announced 20 October – Cebu City, Philippines – venue to be announced 21 October – Quezon City, Philippines – venue to be announced 22 October – Dasmariñas, Cavite, Philippines – venue to be announced 23 October – Bali, Indonesia – Gimme Shelter 24 October – Jogjakarta, Indonesia – venue to be announced 25 October – Purworejo, Indonesia – venue to be announced About Schkeuditzer Kreuz Schkeuditzer Kreuz is the solo project of Kieren Hills, who was born in New Zealand and is based in Lawson, in the Blue Mountains of New South Wales, Australia. The project combines electronic body music and industrial with crust and d-beat punk, a sound Hills has described with terms such as “industrial synth crust” and “d-beat raw synth punk”. The debut release was the five-song 12-inch EP “Give Me Nothing”, launched with a 15-date tour across eastern Australia in March 2021. The discography includes the albums “Isolated and Alone” (2021) and “No Life Left” (2023), the latter later repressed on Bad Habit Records. Schkeuditzer Kreuz first toured Japan in June 2024, a run Side-Line covered at the time. In November 2024 the project released a split 7-inch with Decide Today, and the following year issued the split EP “State Violence State Control” with Sydney act Low Life on Winter Garden Records. The third album, “Swan Grinder“, mastered by Martin Bowes of Attrition, followed on 30 August 2025 and was supported by a European tour that September and October. The single “Keep Dancing”, a remix from “Swan Grinder”, was released in June 2026. The October 2026 dates return Schkeuditzer Kreuz to Japan and Southeast Asia with the widest regional spread of the “Swan Grinder” campaign, adding Cambodia, Thailand, Singapore, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines to the itinerary alongside Japan.

items.body: Industrial group SPK, performing under the name The SPKtR, tours Europe from 7 November to 6 December 2026, with dates across 12 countries: Poland, Denmark, Sweden, Austria, Germany, Hungary, Croatia, Slovenia, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium and Greece. The run includes appearances at the Wrocław Industrial Festival, the XXII Congresso Post Industriale and BIMFEST. SPK is fronted by founding member and film composer Graeme Revell, joined by his son Robert J. Revell. Ticket details are handled by the individual venues and festivals. The tour opens at the Wrocław Industrial Festival in Poland on 7 November, then moves through Scandinavia, Austria and Germany, with festival stops at the XXII Congresso Post Industriale in Pordenone, Italy, on 28 November and at BIMFEST in Sint-Niklaas, Belgium, on 5 December, before closing in Athens on 6 December. Tour dates for The SPKtR 7 November – Wrocław, Poland – Stary Klasztor, Wrocław Industrial Festival 10 November – Copenhagen, Denmark – Loppen 12 November – Gothenburg, Sweden – Monument 031 13 November – Stockholm, Sweden – Nalen, Klubb Död 16 November – Vienna, Austria – Viper Room, Liccht 17 November – Leipzig, Germany – Hellraiser 21 November – Budapest, Hungary – S1 Beer Factory 22 November – Zagreb, Croatia – Boogaloo 23 November – Kranj, Slovenia – TrainStation SubArt 28 November – Pordenone, Italy – Capitol, XXII Congresso Post Industriale 1 December – Augsburg, Germany – Rockfabrik 2 December – Berlin, Germany – Urban Spree 3 December – Utrecht, Netherlands – De Helling 5 December – Sint-Niklaas, Belgium – De Casino, BIMFEST 6 December – Athens, Greece – Black Temple About SPK and The SPKtR SPK formed in Sydney, Australia, in 1978 around New Zealand-born Graeme Revell and Neil Hill, taking its name from Sozialistisches Patientenkollektiv, a German radical-patients’ collective. The debut album, “Information Overload Unit”, followed in 1981, credited to Operator (Revell) on synthesizers, rhythms, treatments and vocals, Mike Wilkins on guitar, bass and tapes, Tone Generator (Dominic Guerin) on synthesizers and treatments, and Mr Clean (Ashley Revell) as technician. “Leichenschrei” followed in 1982 on Thermidor Records in the United States and in 1983 on the band’s own Side Effekts label in the United Kingdom. Sinan Leong joined on lead vocals in 1983, and the group moved toward a more commercial industrial dance sound on the single “Junk Funk” and the album “Machine Age Voodoo” (1984). SPK disbanded in 1988. Graeme Revell went on to a career as a film and video-game composer, scoring titles including “The Crow”, “The Craft”, “From Dusk Till Dawn”, “Sin City”, “Blow” and “Dune”, and contributing to the “Call of Duty” franchise. In 2025 he reactivated SPK for its first live shows in almost four decades, performing in Europe with his son Robert. The pair released the single “The Last of Men” in March 2026 under the name The SPKtR, its first new material in close to forty years, and made their live debut as The SPKtR at Wave-Gotik-Treffen in Leipzig in May 2026. Robert J. Revell also released his own album, “Torn Remnants of Nobility”, in November 2025. The November-December 2026 European tour follows that live debut and the “The Last of Men” release.

items.body: Orquídeas em Prosa, the harsh EBM and dark electro project from João Pessoa, Brazil, releases its new single “Lady Death” on September 18, 2026, on Bandcamp. The track marks the project’s expansion into a duo, with Tony joining founder Soturna Cröstä, and features backing vocals from Luiza “Lizard” Marculino. Lady Death by Orquídeas em Prosa ‘Lady Death’ pushes the bass toward German aggrotech Soturna Cröstä handles vocals, synths, drums and bass on “Lady Death”, with Tony credited for the lyrics. The track was recorded, mixed and mastered by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim HomeStudio, with Luiza “Lizard” Marculino’s backing vocals recorded separately. Orquídeas em Prosa describes the single as pushing the bass further forward than on earlier releases, in the style of German aggrotech, layered under the project’s usual mix of harsh EBM and dark electro. “Lady Death” is also available to stream on Soundcloud. Orquídeas em Prosa’s music continues to explore the darker edges of technological progress through an anarchist, cyberpunk lens, alongside existential crises, warfare and revolution. The project remains entirely self-produced, with Soturna Cröstä handling recording and mixing and cover art supplied by visual artist reptilian.creates. A second single, “Beijo Nuclear”, is scheduled for October 16, 2026. It is currently available to preview on Soundcloud ahead of a wider release. About Orquídeas em Prosa Orquídeas em Prosa is a harsh EBM and dark electro project from João Pessoa, Brazil, started by Soturna Cröstä. The project released its self-titled debut EP on February 3, 2026, a three-track collection recorded solo by Soturna Cröstä at Carmesim Home Studio, with cover art by reptilian_draw. A second EP, “Ilegalismo Electro”, followed on July 17, 2026, again written, performed and produced solely by Soturna Cröstä. For “Lady Death”, Orquídeas em Prosa became a duo with the addition of Tony on lyrics, alongside a guest vocal credit for Luiza “Lizard” Marculino. The project describes its sound as harsh EBM and dark electro filtered through an anarchist, cyberpunk lens, addressing technological progress, existential crises, warfare and revolution, and operates on a DIY basis, self-producing its recordings and artwork. Orquídeas em Prosa is active on Instagram and posts its catalog, including its self-titled EP and “Ilegalismo Electro”, on Bandcamp.

items.album: Dernière Volonté returns to its roots on new album ‘Cendre’
items.excerpt: French post-industrial project Dernière Volonté releases its new album, “Cendre”, on 25 September 2026, in digipak CD, black vinyl and a limited edition of 250 copies on translucent crystal-blue vinyl. “Cendre” returns to the dense, nocturnal and melancholic atmosphere of Dernière Volonté’s earliest work, revisiting the industrial and dark ambient tone the project carried before its shift toward song-based writing on “Les Blessures de l’Ombre” in 2
items.body: French post-industrial project Dernière Volonté releases its new album, “Cendre”, on 25 September 2026, in digipak CD, black vinyl and a limited edition of 250 copies on translucent crystal-blue vinyl. “Cendre” returns to the dense, nocturnal and melancholic atmosphere of Dernière Volonté’s earliest work, revisiting the industrial and dark ambient tone the project carried before its shift toward song-based writing on “Les Blessures de l’Ombre” in 2003 and “Devant le Miroir” in 2006. The twelve tracks are “Harmonies”, “Vanités”, “Maudits”, “Mandoline”, “L’Âne et le Roi”, “Ombres”, “Des Questions”, “Contre Jour”, “Les Jets de Pierres”, “Plus j’y pense”, “Les Jardins de Tannhäuser” and “Célébration (bien à toi)”. The crystal-blue vinyl edition comes with a printed innersleeve and a download code, while the CD edition ships in a 16-page booklet. “L’Âne et le Roi” is the second track shared ahead of the album, following “Célébration (à toi…)”. Both tracks carry forward the martial rhythms, electronics and voice that have defined the project’s sound since the 1990s, applied here to the darker, sparer arrangements of Dernière Volonté’s formative albums. Dernière Volonté’s extended back catalogue remains available alongside the new album, including “Cristal”, “Commémoration”, “Devant le Miroir”, “Frontière”, “Immortel”, “Le Feu Sacré”, “Mon Meilleur Ennemi”, “Ne Te Retourne Pas” and “Prie pour Moi”. About Dernière Volonté Dernière Volonté is the project of French musician Geoffroy Delacroix, known publicly as Geoffroy D., formed in the mid-1990s. The project’s debut release, “Obéir et Mourir”, arrived in 1998 as a limited cassette rooted in martial industrial and dark ambient, built on militaristic rhythms, historical samples and sparse vocals. “Le Feu Sacré” followed in 2001, still within that early industrial and dark ambient mode. Dernière Volonté’s sound changed direction with “Les Blessures de l’Ombre” in 2003, which applied the project’s martial rhythms to verse-chorus song structures and pop melodies for the first time. “Devant le Miroir” continued that shift in 2006, combining drums, synthesizers and dark textures with more intimate melodies. Geoffroy Delacroix expanded his output in 2008 with Position Parallèle, an electronic side project with Pierre Pi mixing EBM and minimal wave, which has released five studio albums to date including “Néons Blancs” (2013), “En Garde à Vue” (2017) and “Aiguille à Découdre” (2024). Dernière Volonté’s own discography continued with “Immortel” (2010), “Mon Meilleur Ennemi” (2012), “Prie pour Moi” (2016), “Frontière” (2019) and “Cristal” (2022). With “Cendre”, the project returns to the darker, more atmospheric register of its first records while keeping the melodic voice it built up over three decades.

Perón produced the album’s tracks, while Melting Rust Opera’s Stefan Bahn
items.body: Swiss electronic musician Carlos Perón and German industrial project Melting Rust Opera released their debut full-length collaboration, “Ultra Haunted Overdrive”, on 7 August 2026 through Dark Daze Music. The ten-track album follows two prior joint singles, “Start Again” and “I’m a Ghost”, and gathers a further eight tracks the pair produced over roughly a year of work. Perón produced the album’s tracks, while Melting Rust Opera’s Stefan Bahners handles vocals and lyrics throughout. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” runs just under 43 minutes and opens with “Quick and Dirty”, followed by “I’m a Ghost”, “An Other Crime”, “Get the Night Out of Your Head”, “Clean Up”, “It’s Not OK”, “The Disasters We Face”, “I Will Adore You”, “Start Again” and the closing “One Star”. The record brings an industrial rock sound that mixes aggressive guitar structures with electronic production and noise elements, moving between brutal and melancholic registers across its ten tracks. The two singles carried over from earlier releases were both already covered on Side-Line: “I’m a Ghost” appeared as a standalone single on 10 December 2025, and “Start Again”, produced by Perón with vocals and lyrics from Bahners, opened the collaboration on 2 May 2025. A third advance track, “An Other Crime”, followed as a single on 13 March 2026 before landing on the album. Carlos Perón and Melting Rust Opera’s collaboration history Perón and Melting Rust Opera had already worked together before their first joint single. Perón contributed to “Manipuliert – Carlos Peròn Trümmer Mischung” on Melting Rust Opera’s 2023 EP “Neue Trümmer”, and mastered the band’s 2024 album “The Power Of I Don’t Care”, also released on Dark Daze Music. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” is the first release credited jointly to both acts as a full-length collaboration. About Carlos Perón Carlos Perón is a Swiss electronic musician from Zurich, one of the three founding members of the legendary Swiss synth-pop trio Yello, formed with Boris Blank and Dieter Meier in 1979. He left the group in 1983 to pursue a solo career spanning electronic experiments, film soundtracks and conceptual releases on labels including Ralph Records, Dark Daze Music and SPV. Early solo works include “Impersonator” (1981) and the soundtrack “Die Schwarze Spinne” (1983), followed by a series of conceptual releases through the 1990s and 2000s. Perón founded the Eisenberg label in the late 1980s and launched the “Der Eisenberg Sampler” compilation series, later revived with Norwegian label Sub Culture Records. He also works as a producer and mastering engineer, having worked with acts including Punch ‘n’ Judy and Piston Damp, and with Beborn Beton in Switzerland and Cologne. Through 2025 and into 2026, Perón has released a run of metal-leaning singles under his Dark Daze Music imprint, alongside his ongoing work with Melting Rust Opera. About Melting Rust Opera Melting Rust Opera is an experimental industrial and metal project based in Rheinbach, Germany, centered on musician and producer Stefan Bahners, with Wilson May contributing live percussion. The project emerged in late 2016 or early 2017 after Bahners’ earlier project, Die Rostigen Löffel, went on hiatus, and combines industrial, avant-garde and noise elements with rock and metal structures. Melting Rust Opera’s discography includes the full-lengths “The Rise and Fall of Flesh Wire” (2021) and “different places” (2022), the EP “Neue Trümmer” and the release “Broken Zukunft” in 2023, and “The Power Of I Don’t Care” (2024). The project has also released remix work, including a version of Laibach’s “Bossanova” (2017), two remixes for Dagobert’s single “Das Mädchen aus der schönen Welt”, a remix of Anne Clark’s “Orange Suns” for “Synaesthesia – Classics Reworked”, and a remix of A Place To Bury Strangers’ “I’m Hurt” for “See Through You: Rerealized”. “Ultra Haunted Overdrive” extends the project’s ongoing work with Perón into its first joint album.

The English post-punk and gothic rock band released “Turn to the Sky” as a single in February 1986 on London Records, and the version now being reissued is the re-recording made the following year for the John Hughes film “Some Kind of Wonderful.” The r
items.body: The March Violets reissue “Turn to the Sky” b/w “Miss Amanda Jones” on digital services on September 18, 2026, and have added a second run of tour dates across the UK, continental Europe and Brazil. The English post-punk and gothic rock band released “Turn to the Sky” as a single in February 1986 on London Records, and the version now being reissued is the re-recording made the following year for the John Hughes film “Some Kind of Wonderful.” The reissue pairs that 1987 film version of “Turn to the Sky” with “Miss Amanda Jones,” a cover of the Rolling Stones song that the band recorded for the same soundtrack. Both tracks had previously been available only on the film’s soundtrack album. Producer Stephen Hague, working from the band’s 1986 original, re-recorded “Turn to the Sky” for the film, and the band performed the song on screen, spending two weeks on the production’s Hollywood set. “Some Kind of Wonderful,” directed by Howard Deutch and written and produced by John Hughes as a follow-up to his 1986 hit “Pretty in Pink,” stars Lea Thompson as Amanda Jones, the character the film’s title track and the Rolling Stones cover both reference. The tour, billed as the second leg of the “Unnatural History” run, follows 14 UK dates the band played in June and July 2026 in support of their “Natural History” album reissue. Alongside that 1980s catalogue, the band also performs songs from Crocodile Promises, their 2024 album, and have said a further album is half-finished. Tour dates for The March Violets October 27, 2026 – Prague, Czechia – Lucerna Music Bar October 31, 2026 – Whitby, UK – Tomorrow’s Ghosts Festival, Pavilion Theatre November 1, 2026 – Newcastle-upon-Tyne, UK – The Cluny November 3, 2026 – Edinburgh, UK – Speakeasy November 5, 2026 – Derby, UK – The Hairy Dog November 6, 2026 – Huddersfield, UK – Amped November 8, 2026 – Bedford, UK – Esquires November 10, 2026 – London, UK – New Cross Inn November 11, 2026 – Brighton, UK – Komedia February 6, 2027 – Sao Paulo, Brazil – Wave Festival Ticket and merchandise links for the dates are listed on the band’s official site. About The March Violets The March Violets formed in Leeds in December 1981, when guitarist Tom Ashton, bassist Laurence “Loz” Elliott, and singers Simon “Detroit” Denbigh and Rosie Garland met at Leeds University. Sisters of Mercy singer Andrew Eldritch released the band’s debut EP, “Religious as Hell,” on his Merciful Release label on August 28, 1982. Seven March Violets singles reached the UK Indie Chart, and the 1984 compilation “Natural History” reached number three on that chart. Cleo Murray replaced Garland as the band’s main vocalist from the 1983 single “Snakedance” onward. In 1986 the band signed to the major label London Records and released “Turn to the Sky,” written by Murray, Elliott and Ashton, as its final single before splitting. The band, by then made up of Ashton, Elliott, drummer Andy Tolson and Murray, went on to record and perform “Turn to the Sky” and “Miss Amanda Jones” for the 1987 film “Some Kind of Wonderful.” The band reunited in 2007 for a one-off Leeds show with Denbigh, Garland and Ashton, joined by Matt Thorpe (of Isolation Division) on bass, and reformed again in 2010. That lineup of Garland, Ashton and Thorpe released a five-CD boxset in 2022 and the album Crocodile Promises on Metropolis Records on July 19, 2024. The reissue of “Turn to the Sky” and “Miss Amanda Jones,” and the new tour dates announced alongside it, follow that album and this year’s “Natural History” reissue and its accompanying UK tour.

items.body: New Zealand electronic rock band Robots In Love will release “Cease and Desist” on September 25, the second single from their upcoming album OVERRIDE. The Dunedin-based act is the creative partnership of vocalist and producer Elenor Rayner and drummer and producer Alex Burchell, joined again by guitarist Henry Flynn Wall of Rebirth To Ruin, who also featured on their previous single, “Convergence”. “Cease and Desist” is a melodic industrial track about extreme obsession. Rayner said she recently discovered the word “limerence” and began thinking about the inability to control obsession, which led to the line “limerence closes every door“, describing a state where no amount of reasoning can get through. Musically, the track scales back its verses before building into a chorus built on heavier riffs. The single also carries two remixes. Melbourne cyberpunk act Sirus contributes a version that moves through decades of electronic music, opening with an ’80s-style sound, passing through a ’90s R&B-inspired interlude and closing on darker, more futuristic production. Burchell also remixes the track under his own alias, Magnetique, in a more subversive take. “Cease and Desist” follows “Convergence”, released on June 8, 2026 as the lead single from OVERRIDE. “Convergence” has drawn over 41,000 YouTube views and 14,000 Spotify streams, and Robots In Love have paired “Cease and Desist” with an official video as well. About Robots In Love Robots In Love is the New Zealand electronic rock project of vocalist and producer Elenor Rayner and drummer and producer Alex Burchell, based in Dunedin (Ōtepoti). The current lineup came together in 2023, with Rayner and Burchell also working separately on other projects: Rayner has released material as Sobriquet and The Crystalline Effect, while Burchell drums with Angels Unchained and the Dunedin Symphony Orchestra and produces under the name Magnetique. The band mixes industrial rock, dark electro, drum and bass, trip hop, goth, metal and cyberpunk influences into a sound built on layered vocals, heavy guitars and electronic production. Side-Line has followed the band’s release history since 2022, when Robots In Love, then working as a New Zealand-based dark electro act, teamed up with Swedish producer JA/VI. They premiered the “Gossip In Your Head” video in September 2023, followed by an EP and remix video that November. In April 2024, the band premiered the “Unbreakable” video, and in January 2025 followed with the “Crush” video. Robots In Love released their debut album, “Activate!”, on May 23, 2025, reaching number 17 on the Aotearoa chart. “Convergence” arrived in June 2026 as the first single from OVERRIDE, with “Cease and Desist” now set to follow it on September 25.
